#2546. (Mis)judgments in Football Analysis (1/3) – MH

von Next Generation am 26.05.2025 in den Kategorien Uncategorized,Video Analysis mit 4 Kommentaren

Daniel Kahneman was one of the leading psychologists of our time. In his book Thinking, Fast and Slow, he presented extensive insights from his many years of research. This article explores how Kahneman’s findings, along with other insights from behavioral science, can be applied to (strategic and tactical) football analysis.

Kahneman became well known in the field of behavioral economics. Together with his colleague Amos Tversky, he succeeded in combining insights from psychology with those of economics. In 2002, he became the first psychologist to be awarded the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences.

His research challenges the fundamental assumption that humans make rational decisions and that cognitive distortions are primarily driven by emotions. Instead, he argued that systematic thinking errors significantly influence our judgment and decision-making. These systematic errors, known as “biases,” occur in predictable ways under certain conditions.

Kahneman’s work has been applied in fields such as medical diagnosis, the legal system, intelligence analysis, philosophy, statistics, and military strategy. It is therefore a logical step to apply his research to sports analysis, where strategic decisions also play a crucial role.

“I suppose that every author has in mind a situation in which readers of their work might benefit from reading it. I imagine the coffee machine at the office, where colleagues exchange opinions and gossip. My hope is to enrich the vocabulary people use when they talk about the judgments and decisions of others (…).” – Daniel Kahneman; Thinking, Fast and Slow

A mere list of cognitive biases is not sufficient to recognize and avoid distortions in one’s own or others’ decisions. Only through a deeper understanding of their origins and mechanisms can the vocabulary around judgment and decision-making be enriched in Kahneman’s sense. Therefore, this article sheds light on the underlying processes and mechanisms of judgment and decision errors.

We begin by examining the scientifically established dual-process model. Following that, the mechanisms of WYSIATI, substitution, and priming will be explored in the context of football. In addition, the most relevant heuristics and cognitive biases will be applied to football analysis. Finally, we will address individual factors within analysis that contribute to the emergence of bias.

This article is only the first part of a series, which will span at least three essays. The series will examine flawed judgments in football analysis and their causes within a scientific framework informed by behavioral research.

One point should be made clear from the outset: bias (and noise) are present wherever decisions are made, and thus affect even expert judgments within their domain.

This article is based on a German translation of Daniel Kahneman’s work. Accordingly, the quotes cited here may not exactly match the original English wording.

To explain human thinking, Kahneman introduces two hypothetical agents: System 1 and System 2. This model provides a framework for understanding how thought processes work. System 1 is responsible for fast thinking, it operates automatically, intuitively, and with little effort. System 2, on the other hand, governs slow thinking, it works analytically, consciously, and requires effort.

These two systems interact continuously whenever we are awake. System 1 runs constantly and automatically, while System 2 operates in an energy-saving mode, only stepping in occasionally. As a result, System 2 rarely takes control. Typically, System 2 adopts the impressions and intuitions generated by System 1 and accepts its intuitive responses.

The division of labor between the two systems is highly efficient. From an evolutionary perspective, this can be explained by the need to react quickly to threats while also engaging in deliberate, long-term planning. Thus, the automatic System 1 developed primarily for threat detection, while the energy-intensive System 2 evolved to support complex reasoning, though it is less frequently engaged in full.

However, it is particularly System 1 that is susceptible to cognitive biases. Due to its energy efficiency, it is limited in logic and statistical reasoning. It often tends to substitute complex questions with simpler ones. System 2, in turn, tends to adopt these flawed outputs, as it does not always monitor or correct the conclusions generated by System 1.

The following simple and intuitive thinking task illustrates the interplay between System 1 and System 2:

Team A has 62% possession and wins a match 1-0. Team B has 38% possession and loses. Which team was more dominant?

Of course, Team A was more dominant. At least, that’s the intuitive conclusion System 1 leads most people to. However, it neglects the fact that possession is not necessarily a reliable measure of dominance, and that match results are very imprecise indicators of performance. Despite lacking detailed data, System 1 assembles the question into a coherent picture. System 2 supports System 1’s incorrect solution, even though with minimal effort it could have reached the correct conclusion. However, System 2 is not consciously engaged.

From this, it follows that people rely on mental shortcuts, so-called heuristics, to quickly solve complex problems. Heuristics are usually very helpful due to their efficiency but can sometimes lead to errors in judgment, known as biases. This is where the relevance for football analysis arises, as will be shown in the following section.

“A heuristic is, technically defined, a simple procedure that helps us find adequate, though often imperfect, answers to difficult questions.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow

First, I have linked a YouTube video that you should watch:

Even if you are already familiar with the video, its insights are remarkable. On the one hand, it can be concluded that focusing on one task can make us blind to other processes. To see and orient ourselves, we need a certain level of attention. However, the main insight of the video is that we cannot believe we have missed something so obvious. For those who did not see the gorilla, the player leaving the scene, or the curtain changing colors, it is unimaginable not to have noticed such obvious events.

“We can be blind to the obvious, and we are also blind to our blindness.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow

Applied to our football analysis, this once again demonstrates how prone we are to errors. How can we direct our attention to all levels of football tactics when, at the slightest distraction, we don’t even see a gorilla? We are only just beginning to discover many additional dimensions of the game as reference points, alongside spatial considerations in positional play. It is not only individual situations that are overlooked due to lack of attention, but possibly entire dimensions and we may not even be aware of this.

We only realize our mistakes when we can no longer analyze a team with the tools we have. We follow our own subjective beliefs in analysis and overlook other logical conclusions that could have been drawn equally well from the existing data. This problem becomes particularly interesting when assessing tactical risk.

Recall the earlier question where you were asked to judge a team’s dominance based on possession percentages and the match result. System 1 constructed the best story it could from high possession and a win. What was not done, however, was likely questioning what is necessary to authentically assess a team’s dominance. We are blind to what we do not pay attention to.

Hasty conclusions based on limited data form the basis of many heuristics. Kahneman refers to these conclusions as “What You See Is All There Is” (WYSIATI).

“It is easier to fit everything you know into a coherent pattern when you know very little.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow

This central mechanism explains why consistency of information, rather than its completeness, is what primarily shapes our beliefs. Unfortunately, we also interpret information accordingly through our coherence-seeking System 1. Kahneman explains that System 1 is completely insensitive to the quality and quantity of information from which impressions and intuitions arise. System 1 looks for coherent information, while a lazy System 2 fails to check it.

“They did not want more information that might spoil their story. WYSIATI.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow

To start, I have prepared a question that should first be answered:

How successful will Relationism be compared to Positionism in the next ten years in the top 5 leagues?

The answer will follow at the end of this section…

To interpret actions and processes, a complex, multidimensional understanding of the game is necessary. In analysis, we face difficult questions that can be answered on multiple levels. Often, there is not just one correct analysis, but several possibilities which together create an accurate picture.

“I know that I know nothing.” (cf. Plato, Apology 22d: “For I was conscious that I knew practically nothing…” )

Through reflection and the constant questioning of our observations and conclusions, we come closer to the goal of better understanding the game. The ability to accept that there are always new perspectives and interpretations fosters a deeper, more nuanced understanding. Unfortunately, when faced with complex matters, humans intuitively tend to fall into different patterns of thinking.

Kahneman explains that even with complex questions, we rarely seem overwhelmed. We are able to provide answers to questions we do not fully understand. But why is that?

Heuristics, as explained above, can be defined as mental shortcuts. Unfortunately, complex questions must also be answered in an energy-efficient way. Thus, we tend to substitute complex questions with simpler ones. This concept underlying many heuristics is called substitution. Often, we do not even notice that we have replaced a difficult question. However, we then use the answer to the simpler question to respond to the complex one. System 1 strives for the simplest possible answer to a question, while System 2, due to its inertia, does not verify the answer.

“You are not overwhelmed, you don’t have to exert much effort, and you may not even notice that you have not answered the question that was asked of you.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow

The concept of substitution is particularly pronounced when emotions are involved in the actual target question. Emotional attitudes amplify the effect. In the case of the so-called affect heuristic (judgments based on emotions), the interaction between System 1 and System 2 is especially prone to disruption. In the context of emotions and attitudes, System 2 does not act as a self-critic but rather as an advocate for the answer proposed by System 1. It looks for arguments that support its own beliefs.

Let us return to the question posed at the beginning of this section. You most likely found an answer to how successful Relationismus will be in the future. However, instead of systematically thinking through the target question, an answer intuitively came to you that corresponds to your beliefs. The heuristic question you unconsciously answered might have been: How much do I like Guardiola’s Positionismus?

Instead of searching for counterarguments against the intuitive answer, you subsequently searched for arguments that support your beliefs. To make a reliable future prediction, it would actually be necessary to free oneself from prejudices and break down the problem into its components, systematically questioning in which situations relational play is superior to positional play and in which situations the opposite is true. After all, the two philosophies can also be combined.

It can be concluded that substitution, together with WYSIATI, forms two of the most important mechanisms in the interplay of System 1 and System 2 underlying many systematic cognitive errors. The following section will introduce another mechanism: priming.

Priming is a fundamental mechanism that explains how we process information when thinking. Our memory plays a central role in this, more precisely, the way it connects information. This principle is called association.

Kahneman uses a metaphor to explain association: “Like ripples on the surface of a pond, activation spreads through a small part of the vast network of associated representations.” Even a single stimulus can be enough to unconsciously activate adjacent concepts or memories.

A priming effect occurs when a specific stimulus, a word, an image, a situation, etc. unconsciously activates certain content in memory. This automatic chain of activation influences how we think, feel, or act without us noticing. The brain essentially lays down mental pathways in the associative network, thereby facilitating the unconscious retrieval of information.

To illustrate, here is a simple example: “If you have recently seen or heard the word eat, you will be temporarily more likely to complete the word fragment so_p as soup rather than soap. The opposite would happen if you had just seen the word wash.”– Thinking, Fast and Slow

Priming is already being used effectively in football contexts. For example, tactical training that includes video analysis and corresponding training formats represents a form of priming. By showing (tactical) videos during team meetings or recreating game-like patterns in training sessions, players can recognize familiar situations during matches, allowing them to react more quickly and effectively. Training decision-making under pressure and developing speed of action can therefore be linked to the priming effect.

Another well-known example of this effect is the “Florida effect.” For those interested in reading more, I’ve linked the original 1996 study by John A. Bargh, Mark Chen, and Lara Burrows.

Priming also plays a role in many other areas of football. It can be deliberately used to create positive outcomes, but it can also have unintended negative effects. Depending on the context, different types of priming are distinguished, such as semantic priming, affective priming, goal priming, and many more. In football, priming is also used, for example, in injury prevention and rehabilitation.

Priming can also be used for the cognitive preparation of a match. In the so-called “Moments of Excellence,” players consciously recall their best past performances immediately before a game. Particularly interesting is the application of “success priming” by the coach, through the use of specific words or phrases in the pre-match talk. Attached is a 2006 study by Stajkovic, Locke, and Blair on this topic, specifically on the unconscious performance enhancement through goal activation.

Analysts, too, are subject to unconscious priming. A glance at the final score before conducting an analysis primes their expectations and subtly shifts the approach toward explaining the outcome, even though the final score, due to its inaccuracy as a performance indicator, says little about a team’s actual dominance.

Given the scope of the subject, an entire article could likely be written solely on the use of priming in football. In this article, however, the foundations of priming are used to understand it as one of the mechanisms underlying cognitive biases that affect football analysis.

“They were primed to find flaws, and that is exactly what they found.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow

Note: An earlier version mentioned the so-called “Florida Effect.” This belongs to a group of priming phenomena that, in the context of the replication crisis, have been only weakly or not at all confirmed. Those interested in learning more can find further information in the comment section. Many thanks to “AG” for the attentive feedback!

At the beginning of the introduction, I explained that distortions in our thinking and decision-making occur in predictable ways under certain conditions. By now, you should have developed a basic understanding of how our thinking is governed by the interaction between System 1 and System 2, how intuitive judgments arise in the process of analysis, and how mechanisms such as WYSIATI, substitution, and priming can specifically contribute to systematic biases in football analysis.

So far, around 200 cognitive biases have been identified. However, unlike many other articles that present a long list of biases with only brief descriptions, I deliberately refrain from doing so here. In my view, a simple enumeration does little to help recognize or avoid these distortions in practice. Instead, I focus on a small number of key biases that are particularly relevant to football analysis. Part 2 of this series will examine additional biases in the context of overconfidence.

“Coherence means that you’re going to adopt one interpretation in general. Ambiguity tends to be suppressed. This is part of the mechanism that you have here that ideas activate other ideas and the more coherent they are, the more likely they are to activate to each other. Other things that don’t fit fall by the wayside. We’re enforcing coherent interpretation. We see the world as much more coherent than it is.” – Daniel Kahneman, Edge

What Kahneman describes here is the phenomenon called associative coherence. The processing of subjectively fitting information is facilitated by associative memory, while the processing of mismatching information is hindered. System 1 thus generates a coherent pattern of activated ideas in associative memory.

This phenomenon inevitably leads to errors in analysis. We should be aware that our analysis alone will never capture the entirety of the subject being analyzed. The analysis is always an expression of the analyst’s beliefs and the ideas activated in their associative memory. Even though System 2 can counteract when activated, it is still influenced by System 1. The concept of associative coherence is therefore closely related to WYSIATI and priming.

As part of the outcome of associative coherence, confirmation bias can be seen. It describes our tendency to want to confirm our existing beliefs.

“The coherence of associative activation induces a confirmatory bias when people examine a hypothesis by increasing the accessibility of hypothesis-consistent information. For example, the intention to test the proposition that ‘Sam is friendly‘ preferentially activates evidence of Sam’s friendliness, whereas testing the proposition that ‘Sam is not friendly‘ preferentially evokes instances of hostile behavior.” – Associative Processes in Intuitive Judgement

In analysis, we tend to seek out, select, and interpret information in a way that confirms our expectations. This, of course, applies to all areas of football analysis. Active countermeasures are necessary to avoid overlooking data that contradicts one’s own hypothesis.

To simplify the illustration of anchoring, please answer the following two questions one after the other.

Does Cristiano Ronaldo have more or less than 1,200 international matches for the senior national team?

How many international matches for the senior national team has Cristiano Ronaldo played?

You have very likely come to the conclusion that Ronaldo has played fewer than 1,200 international matches. Nevertheless, this value probably influenced your estimate of the second question towards a number that is too high. Ronaldo has (as of March 2025) played 219 international matches.

Judgments are often based on the first piece of information given, the anchor. This biases the estimate in its direction. Daniel Kahneman distinguishes two psychological mechanisms that explain this effect.

The anchoring effect is measured and demonstrated in most psychological studies using numerical estimates, for example by estimating prices or probabilities. However, such quantitative judgments are not directly present in video analysis in football. To nevertheless apply the anchoring effect to this context, a change of perspective is useful: Richards J. Heuer Jr., among others a former CIA analyst, investigated the influence of cognitive biases, including the anchoring effect, on qualitative judgment processes within the intelligence community. In his book Psychology of Intelligence Analysis, Heuer deliberately does not refer only to mere numerical estimates, but to all kinds of ongoing judgments or assessments that an analyst inherits from predecessors or gradually revises themselves. Empirical evidence for the effectiveness of anchoring effects in sports video analysis is still lacking, but an analogy via the intelligence community is plausible.

As already described above, the match result provides the analyst with the first available piece of information, acting as a kind of anchor. A 4–0 or 2–1 score leads us to attribute tactical superiority to the winning team and to base our tactical assessments too strongly on the result.

“We should, in any case, assume that every number presented to us has an anchoring effect on us (…).” – Thinking, Fast and Slow

Another example of an anchoring effect in video analysis can be found when analyzing multiple matches of a team. The first game analyzed sets an initial assessment of the team’s tactical approach. As the analysis progresses, the analyst may need to revise their judgments but often fails to adjust sufficiently and remains primarily anchored to the initial assessment. This results in a biased analysis skewed toward the anchor game.

„Even when analysts make their own initial judgment, and then attempt to revise this judgment on the basis of new information or further analysis, there is much evidence to suggest that they usually do not change the judgment enough.” – Psychology of Intelligence Analysis

It is not surprising that people look for reference points when faced with complex issues, the anchor provides exactly this orientation. Unfortunately, in certain cases, it distorts our decision-making. Mussweiler and Strack investigated in their study “Overcoming the Inevitable Anchoring Effect: Considering the Opposite Compensates for Selective Accessibility” how the anchoring effect can be mitigated. Simply being aware of the anchor and the effect is unfortunately not enough to avoid the bias. Instead, a strategy of deliberately thinking about the opposite proves effective in preventing it. Imagine, instead of a 4–0 victory, a 0–4 defeat, and consider how your analysis would look in that case.

Outcome Bias describes the tendency to judge performance based on the outcome. It is closely related to the principle of anchoring. The result serves as an anchor that shifts the judgment in its direction.

Unlike the example mentioned above regarding bias from the match result, Outcome Bias can be applied to all types of results. This means that individual actions and sequences by players are evaluated based on their success or failure, regardless of the actual quality of execution.

An example of this is a successful pressing sequence that leads to winning the ball. Because of the positive outcome, the pressing is overall rated as good. However, other relevant factors, such as intensity, timing, the opponent’s reaction, etc. are either not considered at all or only insufficiently taken into account.

If the same pressing sequence is executed again in a different game situation but fails to win the ball, the pressing is suddenly rated as poor, even though the execution was identical. This bias demonstrates how strongly the evaluation is influenced by the outcome rather than by the quality of the action itself. All actions in the game can be subject to Outcome Bias in analysis.

To prevent Outcome Bias, the evaluation criteria should be adjusted. Instead of judging a performance by its outcome, the process quality should be assessed. This increases the likelihood of future successful actions.

The availability heuristic describes a cognitive shortcut in which people assess the frequency or likelihood of events based on how easily examples come to mind. In doing so, the original question: “How often does an event occur?” is replaced by a simpler one: “How easily can I recall relevant examples?”. This is a typical example of the substitution mechanism.

More important for the availability of an action than the number of examples one can recall is how easily they come to mind, what is known as ease of retrieval. A paradoxical example illustrating the effect of the availability heuristic was demonstrated by Schwarz et al. in 1991: people are less convinced by a decision when asked to list as many arguments in favor of it as possible. This approach plays the two factors, number of arguments and ease of retrieval, against each other: the more arguments that must be generated, the harder they are to retrieve.

In the context of football analysis, this heuristic can lead to an overestimation of certain in-game actions or patterns, particularly during live matches. Striking, prominent, or emotional moments are more easily remembered and therefore disproportionately influence our overall evaluation of the game, regardless of how frequent or relevant they actually were. The availability heuristic has a particularly strong impact on our perception of risk (explored in Part 2).

The game scenes most readily accessible to the analyst are also heavily influenced by their subjective experiences. A wide range of impressions, such as those from previous roles, past matches, or preferred playing philosophies, shape which factors and thus which moments are emphasized in the analysis. A strong bias toward particular strategies, such as overloads in possession, can distort the analysis by neglecting other decisive elements like timing. This simply stems from the complexity and diversity inherent to football. In this way, personal experience encourages subjective conclusions through the combination of the availability heuristic and WYSIATI.

The representativeness heuristic describes judgments about probability based on how representative something appears to be. Representativeness here refers to stereotypes and perceived similarity. When asked about probability, people often engage in substitution, evaluating plausibility instead of actual likelihood. Kahneman illustrates this with the following example:

“You see a person reading The New York Times on the New York subway. Which of the following is a better bet about the reading stranger?

While the more plausible story might lead you to bet on the PhD, you should consider the base rates. Given that far more people without a college degree ride the New York subway than people with doctorates, the statistically sounder bet would be on the person not having a college degree. This example highlights the tension between base rate information and representativeness.

“The representativeness heuristic is misleading when it causes people to ignore base rate information that points in a different direction.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow

Kahneman accordingly advises questioning the informativeness of data and anchoring probability judgments to plausible base rates. To further illustrate the relevance of this concept in a football context, consider the following recent example:

At the beginning of the 2024/25 season, Bayern Munich employed an aggressive, man-marking high press. This tactical approach faced heavy criticism, primarily due to the potential for conceding counterattack goals. Despite the fact that several clubs, such as Atalanta Bergamo, had already been successfully using man-marking in high pressing for years on the international stage, the approach was viewed as atypical in Germany. Since the 1990s, man-marking had largely been replaced in the Bundesliga by zonal marking or hybrid forms. The evaluation of Bayern’s pressing was guided by historical prototypes of man-marking, particularly those involving a libero and, thus, a structural numerical inferiority. Although the man-marking was implemented in a completely different tactical fashion, the comparison seemed plausible due to the similarity and influenced judgments about its success.

In reality, the base rates painted a different picture: Bayern dominated their early Bundesliga matches, prevented opponents from gaining a foothold, and significantly limited their scoring opportunities. Statistically, the approach was highly successful: in their first 11 matches, 7 opponents failed to exceed an xG value of 0.5. The previous season’s champions, Leverkusen, only managed an xG of 0.17 and just 27% possession.

Nonetheless, the assessment of Bayern’s man-marking pressing was distorted by the representativeness heuristic: instead of evaluating the actual likelihood of success based on objective data, the plausibility of an outdated playing style was used as the basis of judgment. This illustrates how stereotypical mental models can lead to misjudgments and how crucial it is to critically examine information in football analysis.

For the sake of completeness, it should be mentioned that individual statistics (base rates in football) are not necessarily meaningful on their own. However, a combination of multiple statistics and data points can produce a more reliable picture to guide analysis. While xG values (as a combination of several data inputs) are still prone to error and need to be contextualized, they can nonetheless provide valuable insights into a team’s actual performance over time.

The conjunction fallacy is one of the cognitive errors that arise from the representativeness heuristic. It describes the tendency of people to judge the combination of two events as more likely than one of the events alone, even when directly compared. The prerequisite is that the combination creates a more coherent and plausible story than the single event. One of the most controversial and well-known examples is the “Linda problem” by Kahneman and Tversky:

“Linda is 31 years old, single, outspoken and very bright. She majored in philosophy. As a student, she was deeply concerned with issues of discrimination and social justice, and also participated in anti-nuclear demonstrations.

Linda is a bank teller and is active in the feminist movement.”

Despite the intuitive plausibility that Linda’s characteristics align more closely with the feminist movement, the first option is statistically more probable. After all, the conjunction of two events (“Linda is a bank teller and is active in the feminist movement”) is always less likely than one of the events alone (“Linda is a bank teller”).

„The most representative outcomes combine with the personality description to yield the most coherent stories. The most coherent stories are not necessarily the most probable, but they are plausible, and the concepts of coherence, plausibility, and probability are easily confused by the unwary.“ – Thinking, Fast and Slow

The “less-is-more pattern” by Christopher Hsee ties into this problem. For those who want to read more, I’ve linked the relevant study here. It states that the probability of the broader event (e.g., Linda is a bank teller) must be higher than that of the event that is included within it (e.g., Linda is a bank teller and active in the feminist movement). However, the more plausible event (less comprehensive) is judged to be more probable than the less plausible, more comprehensive one. This creates the “less-is-more” pattern. As a result, the probability estimate for the more detailed scenario is higher, even though this contradicts logical reasoning.

“This is the trap for forecasters and their clients: the more detailed the scenarios, the more convincing they are, but the less probable they become.” – Thinking, Fast and Slow

In the context of opponent team analysis for an upcoming match, the analyst must be aware that they are the forecaster, making probability estimates about the opponent’s future style of play. Thus, they should assess the likelihood of events, not merely their plausibility.

Applying Hsee’s “less-is-more principle” to this context means that detailed, plausible match scenarios may sound impressive, but are statistically less reliable for prediction than broader descriptions. Each additional assumption in a forecast multiplies individual probabilities and thereby reduces the overall likelihood of an accurate prediction.

However, this is not a call for a lack of detail in opponent analysis. On the contrary, the more detailed, precise, and comprehensive the analysis, the better the ability to derive general playing principles, patterns, and behaviors of the opponent. Therefore, the analyst should aim to analyze the opponent as holistically as possible before making generalized statements that increase the predictive probability.

While in Part 2 I will address structural conditions in football that affect the intuition of analyst and coach experts, in this section I will focus on the individual conditions of different types of analysis. Even though I speak here about football analysis in general, it is important to clarify that there are various forms of analysis in football (see table). Different types of analysis also have different individual susceptibilities to cognitive biases.

Certain biases are additionally triggered by specific types of analysis. Prediction, for example, is particularly affected by the representativeness heuristic, since it involves assessing probabilities. Team analysis over multiple games increases susceptibility to the anchoring heuristic, and post-match analysis is prone to hindsight bias, the tendency to overestimate the predictability of an event after it has occurred.

Similarly, focusing on a single level of analysis increases vulnerability to WYSIATI. You should now be familiar with the cognitive errors mentioned here, so they should not come as a surprise. One factor not yet addressed in this article, which demonstrably increases susceptibility to all biases, is time pressure. Time pressure plays a significant role especially during live analysis, though not exclusively.

Time pressure forces analysts to make quicker decisions. Research shows that under such conditions, people rely more heavily on heuristics, increasing the likelihood of errors. Among other studies, Finucane et al. (2000) examined the influence of the affect heuristic on the evaluation of benefits and risks, demonstrating that time pressure amplifies this effect.

Analysts therefore have to rely more on their intuition during live analysis. This brings me to Part 2, where I will identify conditions that increase experts’ susceptibility to intuitive errors.

By now, it should be clear why we delve so deeply into the mechanisms of heuristics. Without a fundamental understanding of how they work, heuristics and cognitive biases are difficult to recognize.

Many behavioral psychology insights can be profitably applied in sports analysis. This includes not only heuristics and cognitive biases but can also be extended to other areas of football analysis. However, to cover these application areas sufficiently, there will be a Part 2, Part 3, and, if necessary, a Part 4.

In Part 2, I will address the topic of overconfidence. Among other things, it will examine the susceptibility of expert intuition as well as risk strategies and risk assessments in football. Strategies for avoiding biases in football analysis will also be presented.

Part 3 (and possibly Part 4) will focus on “noise” in football analysis. Unlike bias, noise does not describe the distortion of judgments in a particular direction but the unconscious variability of multiple judgments under identical decision conditions.

Next Generation May 29, 2025 um 5:58 pm

If necessary, I may additionally address the replication crisis in psychology in Part 2 for the sake of completeness. However, here is a clarification in advance:

As part of the replication crisis, some studies on well-known psychological phenomena could not be replicated with the same results. Particularly affected was so-called behavioral priming, which assumes that certain stimuli can trigger unconscious changes in behavior. Well-known examples, such as the so-called Florida effect (slower walking after being primed with age-related words) could not be confirmed in independent replications. By now, a large portion of such behavioral priming effects is considered non-robust or methodologically questionable.

In contrast, there is another, significantly better-supported understanding of priming, cognitive or semantic priming. Here, a preceding stimulus (prime) influences the processing of a subsequent stimulus, for instance by accelerating or decelerating its recognition. This effect has been reliably demonstrated in numerous experiments. This form of priming is based on the activation of semantic networks in memory and is regarded as a fundamental mechanism of information processing.

Therefore, it is important to distinguish between different types of priming in the context of the replication crisis. While many behavioral priming effects have been empirically refuted or at least significantly relativized, cognitive priming effects, such as activation within the semantic network, remain scientifically recognized and well-supported.

The form of priming described in this article, such as a mechanism behind bias or as an activation cue to improve players’ response speed, is also based on these well-established findings. As mentioned in the article’s section, priming is used here as a mechanism to understand cognitive biases. Overall, it can be concluded that priming remains a recognized phenomenon in psychology, but only when its various forms are considered in a differentiated manner.

#2545. Celtic could demand €20m for Germany midfielder Mika Baur amid interest from Premier League, Bundesliga and Serie A

Things have moved quickly for Mika Baur since he left SC Paderborn to join Celtic FC for a fee of around €6 million last summer.

After hitting the ground running in Scotland, Baur made his senior Germany debut in October, and he was most recently called up to the U21 national team, but was forced to withdraw due to injury.

According to Sky Germany, Baur's development in Scotland has attracted interest from clubs in the Premier League, Bundesliga and Serie A, with the report suggesting that he could become a major transfer target next summer.

With Baur under contract until 2030 and no release clause included in his deal, Celtic are under no pressure to sell and could demand a fee in the region of €15-20 million for the central midfielder, according to the report.

Baur has scored four goals in 19 appearances for Celtic so far.

#2544. Champions Classic NBA Draft guide: Who scouts will be watching in college basketball's high-profile showcase

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The most anticipated double-header of the young college basketball season takes place tonight in Chicago as No. 2 Duke meets No. 5 Michigan State, followed by No. 15 Kansas vs. No. 24 Kentucky in the Champions Classic.

The event is also expected to draw a heavy dose of NBA scouts and decision-makers to Chicago, given the opportunity to see so many high-level prospects under one roof on one night.

One wrinkle: The best NBA prospect on the court Tuesday night won't even be eligible to be drafted in 2027. That's Duke freshman Joaquim Boumtje Boumtje who is 17 years old and won't turn 18 until next May. In order to be eligible for the NBA Draft, a player must be at least 19 years old during the calendar year of the draft, per NBA rules.

So not only will Boumtje Boumtje be ineligible for the upcoming draft; he is expected back at Duke for his sophomore season.

Another thing to keep in mind is that these NBA scouts and executives will use what they see on Tuesday night as a benchmark and something to measure against for the rest of the season. They will not over-index on what they see on just one given night.

The public, on the other hand, has a tendency to fall for that trap. Because tonight is so visible, if someone has a glaring performance (good or bad), it often anchors a lot of the public discourse for the rest of the season. Trevor Keels is the classic example. He scored 25 points in the 2021 Champions Classic, was mocked as a lottery pick almost immediately afterwards, ended up declaring for the draft prematurely, and slipped to the second round.

The moral of the story – keep what you see on Tuesday night in perspective, because the people who make the big decisions certainly will.

So with all that in mind, here's a look at the top NBA prospects from the four teams in action at the Champions Classic

This shouldn't come as a surprise, but the Blue Devils lead the way in terms of total NBA prospects. What's interesting about this year's team though, is that their best prospect, Joaquim Boumtje Boumtje, isn't even eligible this year, but is the early favorite to be the top pick in 2028. Boumtje Boumtje has a combination of size and skill, which is unmatched for his age, not just in college basketball, but anywhere in the world.

Ngongba had a chance to be a first-round pick a year ago, but opted to return to Duke, and so far, it looks a decision that is going to pay off. Ngonba fits a coveted NBA archetype in that he's a mismatch five-man who can play inside and out. He is a vertical spacer, reliable passer, and consistent offensive rebounder who has massive length to also be a rim protector. Scouts want to see him take the next step as a shot-blocker and as a rebounder while proving his durability.

If Ngongba can prove he can space the floor with his shooting, that's just an added bonus. He's prepared for that challenge by getting himself into the best shape of his career and looks poised to be the focal point for the Blue Devils, at least on the interior, this season. In short, it's early, but the lottery is very much in play here.

Sarr is a long and athletic big wing who, last year as a freshman, was already one of the best perimeter defenders in the ACC, if not the country. This year, he's going to get the volume to show his offensive growth. So far, that's come more in transition and as a secondary playmaker, but what the NBA is going to be most interested in is his ability to make spot-up 3s in order to fit that coveted 3-and-D archetype. Sarr was 32% from that range last season, but hasn't even attempted a three through two games this year, but has gotten to the free-throw line in high volume and made 71%, after connecting on only 53% last year.

While the progression of Sarr's total game is important, scouts will be monitoring the shooting most closely all year long. Duke also appears to be recruiting as if they expect Sarr to move on after the year. The first-round should be the expectation, with the late lottery not being out of the question.

Williams has quickly become one of the most polarizing draft prospects in the country. He was a top five recruit out of the high school ranks a year ago because of his combination of size, athleticism, fluidity, skill, and shot-blocking potential, even with real questions about his physicality.

Williams has played a limited role to start the season and could fall further out of the rotation as games get closer. Nevertheless, it wouldn't be at all surprising to see him explore professional opportunities, even if this season doesn't go as expected. It also wouldn't be unprecedented to see a team invest a first-round pick in trying to develop his tools, even in that scenario. It's a trajectory that could mirror that of Peyton Watson, who was a prized 2021 recruit who didn't play much in his freshman season at UCLA, still declared for the draft, and ended up being the 30th pick for the Nuggets a year later. That pick has gone down as a very good one.

If the exhibition slate was any indication, Blackwell may be Duke's most reliable player this season. He came to Durham after putting up 19 points and 5 rebounds on 43/39/86 shooting last year for Wisconsin, but did not get any first-round traction in the pre-draft process.

The narrative once Blackwell hit the portal was that he wanted to play with the ball in his hands. Fortunately, he seems to have gotten over that, because his path to the NBA is based on proving he can be a reliable two-way role player, not an alpha creator. Duke is the biggest stage to prove that. If the shooting splits hold up and he can provide some secondary playmaking and be a defensive asset, then hopefully scouts won't be so worried about his lack of length come the next draft cycle.

NBA scouts are also watching: Deron Rippey Jr., 6-1, freshman, guard; Bryson Howard, 6-4, freshman, guard; Caleb Foster, 6-4, senior, guard; Cayden Boozer, 6-3, sophomore, guard.

The Spartans are unlike many of college basketball's other top programs in that while they are projected to be among the very best teams in the sport, but they don't have as many glaring NBA prospects. Of course, similar claims used to be made about Villanova teams of old, and that proved to be beyond shortsighted, so it's possible that time will prove the masses wrong about the individual talent on this year's team.

Fears is undoubtedly one of the best players and floor generals in all of college basketball. Everything Michigan State does begins with him, and the same was true last year for a team that won 27 games and advanced to the Sweet 16 before running into UConn. There are, however, questions about how his game translates to the NBA. He lacks ideal measurables for the league, doesn't have the outlier burst to compensate, and is also a questionable shooter.

Still, it's hard to bet against Fears' will, and so chances are he figures out how to stick at the next level. The elephant in the room, though, is that while he is a true senior this year at Michigan State, his earning potential will almost certainly be higher in college than the pros next year. The Spartans have recruited as if he's not going to be back, but if and when financial reality hits, will they be willing to tolerate seeing him in another uniform? Only time will tell.

The baby-faced sophomore is still a work in progress and just starting to grow into his body and fill out his frame. Right now, he is much more of a Robin to Fears' Batman for the Spartans. And yet, Scott has a game that could ultimately translate to the next level more seamlessly. He's a big wing with positional size, a reliable floor-spacer who made 37% of his threes last year as a freshman. He's also a reliable decision-maker who turned the ball over a total of 32 times in 729 minutes a year ago. In short, the NBA is intrigued, so whether or not it's this year or down the road, Scott is on the right trajectory.

NBA scouts are also watching: Coen Carr, 6-6, senior, forward; Jasiah Jervis, 6-4, freshman, guard; Ethan Taylor, 7-2, freshman, center.

For the second consecutive year, Bill Self has a freshman with a chance to prove he should be the top pick in the draft. The biggest question for most of the summer, though, was based on who else they could get to surround Tyran Stokes. Now, thanks to eligibility being granted to Melvin Council, Tre White, and Tre Kaufman-Renn, the Jayhawks suddenly have an ideal supporting cast. Here's the thing, though: if those guys were NBA players at this point, they wouldn't have been available to return.

Stokes is the early favorite to be the top pick in the 2027 NBA draft. He's built like a throwback power forward, but can initiate like a guard, not just for himself, but for others as well. The biggest questions in high school were about his approach and ability to impact winning on a daily basis, but so far at Kansas, he's gotten rave reviews. Being surrounded by veterans no doubt helps, as does having some reinforcements. When Stokes dropped 27 points, eight rebounds, and seven assists on Duke in an exhibition, it was a sign of things to come. That performance came without the Jayhawks having yet established an ideal scheme to get him going in space and movement. In short, if Stokes' mindset stays the same, he has a chance to distance himself from the field this season, and that process could begin tonight.

NBA scouts are also watching: Taylen Kinney, 6-2, freshman, guard; Keanu Dawes, 6-9, senior, forward; Melvin Council Jr, 6-4, graduate, guard; Tre White, 6-6, graduate, wing; Trey Kaufman-Renn, 6-8, graduate, center/forward.

Malachi Moreno and Milan Momcilovic both had a good chance to be drafted last June. So, when they opted to return, it wasn't for a lack of options; it was for the valuation that college basketball, and Kentucky in particular, was able to pay them. That's a very different calculus than graduate students who return after not signing NBA contracts. So, while this year's roster may not have any glaring lottery picks, it does have pro talent.

Moreno fits a coveted archetype in today's NBA because he has legit size and can be reliable in offensive structure. He's a quick processor of the game and a reliable decision-maker at various spots on the floor. He's a solid passer, efficient finisher, and may even have some long-term shooting potential. He also provides some defensive rim protection, but could certainly help his stock this season by becoming more assertive around the rim on both ends of the floor. The first-round should be the goal for Moreno coming out of this season.

Momcilovic was one of the best shooters in college basketball last year, making 49% of his threes on almost 8 attempts per game, while also making 88% of his free throws for good measure. Through two games at Kentucky, he's getting even more volume, with 17 attempted threes in just two games so far. While his floor-spacing gravity is not in doubt, the questions for the next level are more about his ability to defend his position without putting his team in rotation. So, all-year scouts will be locked in on some of the nuances of Momcilovic's game, like his foot speed, angles, and rotations. Long-term, Momcilovic has positional size and a translatable niche, but may be in a familiar spot in the off-season, with more guaranteed money in the college ranks.

Wilkins was one of the best mid-major freshmen in the country last year, posting nearly 18 points and 5 assists for a Furman that went to the NCAA Tournament. He's a classic late-bloomer who had an undeveloped, wiry frame in high school, but quickly started to put things together as he grew into his body.

While he's still filling out, Wilkins is naturally smooth with real playmaking genes. Through two games at Kentucky, there's also been an early uptick in his shooting (he's 5-for-11 from three and 6-for-6 from the free-throw line). If that growth is sustainable, he'll continue to build momentum with NBA decision-makers. Exactly what his timeline will be, though, still remains to be seen.

NBA scouts are also watching: Kam Williams, 6-7, junior, wing; Zoom Diallo, 6-5, junior, guard; Mason Williams, 6-2, freshman, guard

#2543. Five under-the-radar MLB free agents who could make a big impact next season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is a little more than a week old now and we're still waiting for the first big trade or free agent signing. That isn't unusual, though. The hot stove, like the regular season, is a marathon, not a sprint. A lockout is expected when the collective bargaining agreement ends at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, and there should be a flurry of activity before then.

We ranked the offseason's top 50 free agents, and although it is not a great class, there are dozens of quality players available. You just have to know where to look. Here now are five players who did not rank among our top 50 free agents, but would nonetheless be good options and solid pickups for teams that want to raise their floor and improve their supporting cast.

It was a tale of two seasons for the 29-year-old Bryan Abreu, who had a 5.81 ERA before the All-Star break and a 1.71 ERA after. The under-the-hood estimators, like FIP and xERA, were better in the second half as well, though Abreu lost close to 2 mph off his fastball this year and, not coincidentally, a whole bunch of swings and misses. Abreu is third in appearances and second in innings among relievers since 2022 and it's possible the workload is catching up to him. There's still enough bat-missing ability and late-inning experience here for Abreu to contribute to a contender's bullpen. It just might happen as a seventh-inning guy moving forward, not as the Moment of Truth™ reliever who pitches in the game's biggest moments.

If you're looking for a bottom of the order guy who will take walks and give you 10-15 home runs, that's J.P. Crawford. His defense, specifically his range and arm, has slipped so much in his early 30s that he's no longer a viable shortstop, though he played 33 games at third base this past season. I like him better at second base, but third base works too. Crawford gets on-base at a decent clip and won't strike out excessively, plus he's long been regarded as an excellent teammate and grade-A clubhouse guy. It seems like his time with the Mariners is over and it's for the best. Crawford can go elsewhere, play a new position, and just be part of the lineup rather than one of the faces of the franchise.

Due to injury and ineffectiveness, it looked like Sean Newcomb was on his way out of baseball two years ago. He then reinvented himself as a sinker/curveball guy and carved out a nice second phase to his career as a workhorse utility reliever who won't beat himself with walks (an early career bugaboo) and will limit hard contact in the air. Newcomb, 33, worked at least 90 innings the last two seasons while pitching in every possible role. He closed out games, worked high leverage as a setup guy, soaked up innings in long relief, and opened a few times as well. Newcomb is likely miscast as a go-to bullpen option, though he can be a valuable third or fourth option for a contender. The utility reliever is all the rage these days and Newcomb fits the profile to a T.

Now 35, Emilio Pagán was sensational after returning from a hamstring injury in July, pitching to a 1.88 ERA with 34 strikeouts and only five walks in his final 28 ⅔ innings. The downside is the same as it's always been: Pagán is exceptionally home run prone (career 1.51 HR/9), which is a bad trait for a late-inning reliever who pitches almost exclusively in close games. His fastball remains firm, though, and his splitter is an elite swing-and-miss pitch that allows him to neutralize righties and lefties. As long as you're willing to live with the home run risk, Pagán remains a capable high-leverage reliever, one who is not out of place pitching important innings for a contending team.

Platoon DHs are not the hottest commodity, but Joc Pederson fills the role about as well as anyone in the game. He's a left-handed hitter, so he's on the heavy side of the platoon, and he authored a .245/.338/.496 line with terrific ball-tracking data (exit velocity, etc.) against righties. If you must play him in the field, Pederson can stand in right field or at first base for about six innings before being subbed out for a defensive replacement. He's essentially a bat-only player, though. Pederson will turn 35 in April and he's still a powerful and productive hitter against righties and an elite clubhouse vibes dude.

#2542. Kirk Cousins trade grades: Vikings hope to salvage offense; Raiders get 'A,' turn to Fernando Mendoza

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Kevin O'Connell and the Minnesota Vikings are making one last-ditch attempt to save their offense, reuniting with Kirk Cousins and sending their 2027 third-round pick to the Las Vegas Raiders in return.

Cousins, 38, was in the middle of a renaissance year in Sin City, with 20 passing touchdowns and just eight interceptions. He is now being called upon to save a dire situation in Minneapolis. The Vikings have scored just 11 offensive touchdowns this season, tied with the Chargers for the fewest in the NFL. Offseason addition Kyler Murray and veteran backup Carson Wentz have both struggled mightily, with Murray at or near the bottom of most major passing categories and Wentz throwing for just 81 yards and two interceptions starting for Murray (hamstring) on "Monday Night Football."

Cousins spent 2018-23 in Minnesota, where he made three of his four career Pro Bowls. He was especially good in 2022, when he led an NFL-high eight game-winning drives, and Minnesota went 13-4 before being bounced in its first playoff game. The next year, Cousins was arguably even better — on pace for maybe the best year of his career — before tearing his Achilles. Now, three years later, he gets to leave a different lasting legacy in Minnesota.

Teammates until Monday, Fernando Mendoza and Cousins now step into very different spotlights. The Raiders will hope the Mendoza era lasts for years to come and that he can make some positive strides this year. The Vikings, on the other hand, are all-in on this year. Here's how both teams fared:

That the Vikings are even in this situation is worthy of an "F." Ever since Cousins left, they have failed to find a suitable replacement: Sam Darnold was excellent in 2024, but the Vikings let him go in favor of J.J. McCarthy. McCarthy played poorly and was hurt several times last year, as the Vikings rode a quarterback carousel. Minnesota traded McCarthy, who had been demoted to third-string behind Murray and Wentz, to the Giants early this season. Murray — always a curious-at-best fit for this offense — clearly wasn't cutting it, and Wentz was never going to, either.

Cousins has been good this year — not great, but good. He looks far better than what he had been in Atlanta, where it was clear his mobility hadn't returned post-Achilles tear. He's still never going to win with his athleticism, but his negative play rate is down to 6.7%, on pace for a career best, and he is only being sacked on 9.8% of his dropbacks, also on pace for a career best. How much of that praise belongs to Klint Kubiak is up for debate, but it's clear Cousins has regained some of his spryness. He doesn't have to be Michael Vick, but he can't be a statue.

Really, though, this all comes down to fit. Murray never fit. Cousins, hypothetically, does. Obviously, there is proof of concept here given his past in Minnesota. He attacks the middle of the field and delivers on intermediate throws. Plus, he is comfortable off play action. These are crucial parts of O'Connell's scheme. Cousins, if nothing else, should do a much, much better job keeping the offense on schedule.

Given the circumstances, this grade can only be so high, and given the solution, it cannot get that much higher. Cousins is not a star. His arm strength is not what it once was, and for all the good things he did in Las Vegas, he is coming off a three-interception game. We'll see how he holds up, physically, over the rigors of an 18-game regular season (he will not get a bye) plus expected postseason. His accuracy is a bit down from his best years, though it's still a clear major improvement over Murray and Wentz, who at times seemed unable to hit water if they fell off a boat.

It's also nice that the Vikings still have a third-round pick — the Eagles' from the Jonathan Greenard trade — next year. It will be better than Minnesota's, too.

Even though Cousins can unlock the best part of this offense — Justin Jefferson, who is the biggest winner of this deal — he cannot fix everything. The offensive line has been up-and-down at best, and the running game has been poor. Minnesota's running backs are 31st in percentage of carries with a missed tackle forced and 26th in EPA per rush. There's not much juice there.

Overall, Minnesota got better with this trade. Much better. But it couldn't get much worse, either. Even with a truly outstanding defense, is average-to-slightly-above-average quarterback play and, in turn, average offense good enough to cash in on Super Bowl aspirations? The Vikings are about to find out, but at least they're giving themselves a chance.

P.S. O'Connell had better be right about this move. He has missed on two straight quarterback evaluations. He cannot miss on a third.

If you told a Raiders fan before the season that Mendoza would make his first start in Week 10, they'd probably say that's about right. If you told them he'd start because the Raiders got a top-100 pick for Cousins, they'd be very happy with that outcome.

Cousins well exceeded the mere placeholder role he was given. He played well and, at times, very well. He kept an offense that's very much in the early building stage moving — the Raiders are eighth in points per drive this season. He did this all alongside one of the league's worst running games and worst/youngest wide receiver corps. He leaned on Brock Bowers, who looks like a superstar once again, and fellow tight end Michael Mayer. The Raiders went 4-5 under Cousins and were competitive in several losses. This was a 99th-percentile outcome.

Now, it's Mendoza's turn. It's a little bit tough to drop him into the starting role in these circumstances — not knowing he's starting until Tuesday, and facing Seattle's ferocious defense — but that will be of little matter in the long haul. Kubiak did a great job with Cousins, and the fruits of his labor are a valuable draft pick as Las Vegas continues its build. Strong work all around.

#2539. Jonathan Taylor stays with Colts: Why Indianapolis demanded a first-round pick

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Jonathan Taylor isn't going anywhere. The Indianapolis Colts decided to keep their 27-year-old, three-time Pro Bowl running back at the 2026 NFL trade deadline. The Colts  turned down offers of second-round picks and more for Taylor, indicating they required at least a first-round pick to trade him away, according to Tom Pelissero.

Basically, it seems like Indianapolis turned down trade offers comparable to what the San Francisco 49ers sent the Carolina Panthers in 2022 to acquire running back Christian McCaffrey, who was 26. Back then, San Francisco sent Carolina the following picks: a 2023 second-round pick, a 2023 third-round pick, a 2023 fourth-round pick and a 2024 fifth-round pick.

So why would the Colts walk away from such a deal for Taylor? Let's break it down.

The Colts are overcompensating in their Taylor trade demands after not getting market value for Quenton Nelson (a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick from the Seattle Seahawks). They also don't have their own first-round pick ahead of the highly anticipated 2027 NFL Draft because they traded it to the New York Jets a year ago to acquire cornerback Sauce Gardner. That's why Indianapolis probably rebuffed trade packages that lacked first-round picks: they were trying to clean up their mistake from last year's trade deadline.

Also, Taylor is one of the best running backs of his generation: he averages the fifth-most rushing yards per game (88.8) in NFL history. It's understandable why Indianapolis maintained the stance that they won't trade him away for anything less than a first-round pick.

The running back contract market has also changed, and they were able to lock Taylor down on a two-year, $44 million extension with $39 million in guaranteed money before the 2026 season began. That's a great value. The Colts now have him locked down through the 2028 season, the rest of his 20s, and there isn't any guaranteed money left on the deal in 2027 or 2028. That makes it really easy to move him via trade in the future or keep him around for whatever quarterback they eventually add to replace Daniel Jones next year. Those are the reasons why Taylor won't be relocating at the 2026 NFL trade deadline on Tuesday afternoon.

#2538. Re-grading the Jaylen Brown-Paul George trade: Celtics' grade has greatly improved, 76ers' mark stays perfect

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Besides the Luka Dončić stunner, you could argue that this summer's Jaylen Brown blockbuster was the most surprising trade in recent NBA history. A former Finals MVP coming off of his best season traded for ... Paul George? Someone widely treated as one of the NBA's worst contracts and half of the draft capital a superstar typically fetches? The reactions were, obviously, extreme. Celtics fans revolted. Pundits expected a meaningful drop-off for Boston. Trade graders like myself pilloried Brad Stevens and his front office for moving a 29-year-old All-NBA forward for what appeared to be far less than fair value.

And yet, as Brown prepares to face his former employer for the first time, the two teams sit neck-and-neck in the Eastern Conference. The 76ers top the standings at 9-2. The Celtics are right behind them at 8-2, but have the East's best net rating at +11.6. While Philadelphia has thus far gotten exactly what it wanted out of the trade, the Celtics seemingly have as well. So with their first of potentially many high-stakes clashes this season set for Tuesday night (8 p.m. ET, NBC/fubo), let's revisit the trade and hand out revised grades for the offseason's most impactful trade.

The backlash to the George-for-Brown trade was fundamentally centered on two premises:

The first premise was, frankly, outdated in the apron era. Yes, Kevin Durant netted four first-round picks, a first-round swap, and players who would go on to net six additional first-round picks and another swap, but that was all the way back in February 2023, and that trade completely derailed Phoenix's future. The James Harden trade played out similarly for the Nets. Teams are more skittish about all-in moves for older players than they've ever been.

There have been outlier, extremely high-cost trades since then, but all came under somewhat irreplicable circumstances. Mikal Bridges netted five first-round picks and a swap, for instance, but he never misses games, came with two years of cheap cost-control and played collegiately with several other key Knicks. New York viewed him as the finishing piece of a championship team, and the Knicks were ultimately proven correct.

Desmond Bane wasn't as underpaid, but he fit the extremely narrow niche the Magic needed: someone who could enhance their offense without commanding high usage on a team that was already locked into two max-salary shot-creators or compromising their defensive identity. There were maybe a handful of players in the NBA Orlando could have targeted for that role, and Bane, amazingly, was probably the only one available. In an extremely injured Eastern Conference, the Magic tried to be opportunistic. That's where these lopsided trades happen. They're almost always circumstantial.

The more typical star trade scenario is something closer to what the Milwaukee Bucks went through with Giannis Antetokounmpo. The player is older, attempts to fix things internally have failed, and the relationship between star and team is no longer tenable. The acquiring team typically has a leverage advantage, and that's especially true in the apron era, where paying the sort of giant salaries these stars get in their early 30s carries far more risk than reward. Antetokounmpo netted three picks, one swap and a handful of players that won't be foundational for the Bucks. We know Antetokounmpo had more trade value than Brown because the Celtics tried to trade Brown and more for Antetokounmpo, but a deal wasn't struck. So if Antetokounmpo, a two-time MVP, was worth three-and-a-half picks plus some player value, Brown being worth two picks and some player value feels in line with the new, cost-conscious NBA.

And then of course, there's the matter of what the player value actually was. That brings us to George. From November through January of last season, George averaged just 16 points on 42-38-86 shooting. This was in line with his 2024-25 performance, and together, the year-and-a-half sample felt reliable for an aging star. Well, George then got suspended 25 games. When he returned in March, he was a 21-point scorer on better shooting splits who looked rejuvenated defensively. He went on to torch the Celtics in the first round of the playoffs. Most of us expected George to look more like the player he was before that suspension in Boston. The Celtics bet that he would look like who he was after, and thus far, they've looked correct.

The raw numbers are superb: 20.4 points, 47-43-81 shooting and his highest assist and rebounding rates since he left the Clippers. The fit has been even better. Much was made of how low many advanced metrics are on Brown relative to his reputation, but the more significant story here was always his outlier status within Boston's intended team structure. Joe Mazzulla wants to maximize 3-point attempt rate. George's 3-point attempt rate so far this season (51.4%) is nearly twice Brown's (27.8%). Brad Stevens spoke openly about not wanting to concentrate usage in two players, and George's usage rate is nearly eight percentage points lower than Brown's was a year ago. The Celtics wanted this sort of player in their system and next to Jayson Tatum, and it's working.

Yet just as vitally, George is helping the Celtics diversify a bit as a team. The Celtics generated the second-fewest turnovers in the NBA last season. They're averaging the eighth-most in the NBA thus far this season, and George is the single biggest reason why. Only Dyson Daniels and Scottie Barnes are averaging more deflections, and among players who have played at least four games, only Daniels and Kris Dunn are generating more steals.

The Celtics had the lowest free-throw attempt rate in the NBA last season as well. They're right around the middle of the pack this year. Tatum is the one drawing most of those fouls, but George is a critical part of the structure that gets Tatum to the line. Brown can be a bit of a ball-stopper. Among true forwards, only Kawhi Leonard and Zion Williamson averaged more seconds per touch than Brown a year ago. The average George touch this season lasts 3.3 seconds compared to just under five for Brown a year ago. It's simply easier to compromise a defense when the ball is moving and players are making quick decisions. That's how defenses are forced into rotation and wind up fouling out of desperation. As a team, the Celtics have the sixth-lowest average time per touch this season compared to the eighth-highest a year ago.

Even the contract feels a bit more palatable now than it did at the time. Brown would have become eligible for an extension on his supermax contract last offseason, and based on the season he had, he would have been more than justified in asking for one. The Celtics, clearly, had no plans to commit extra years to Brown on top of the three that he was already owed. George isn't quite living up to his supermax price tag thus far this season, but his deal is a year shorter and comes with no such extension pressure.

If anything, his player option for next season opens some interesting doors for the Celtics if they decide they're happy with this partnership. As of right now, the Celtics have around $3 million in first-apron room for the 2027-28 season based on current projections. Say they want to use the full mid-level exception on a free agent or perhaps need a bit more wiggle room to make a trade. They could theoretically go to George and ask him to lower his cap figure in exchange for another year of security. Turning a one-year, $56.6 million deal into, say, a two-year, $90 million deal could make sense for both sides provided George sustains this level of play.

The reasonable fear that he might not is why we stop at a "B-" for Boston. This is still his age-36 season. George has been injury-prone for most of his career. He presumably will not get a 25-game break this season, and even if he's this good all year, all of these benefits he's brought to Boston are somewhat regular-season-centric. The playoffs are a different game, one that leans much more into Brown's strengths as an individual shotmaker and man-to-man defender. The Celtics still never get to the rim. Their best answer for opposing star guards is probably Jordan Walsh, whose offense makes him hard to play for too long. If Boston flames out in the playoffs, we might view Brown's absence as one of the bigger reasons why. The path to actually winning this trade gets paved in April and May.

But for now, at least, it's starting to make sense. The Celtics added two premium draft assets in a way that allowed them to maintain their existing playing style and avoid taking a major step back in the present. They sidestepped what probably would have been an ugly contract negotiation, and the more barbs get traded in the press, the clearer it becomes that this situation simply was not salvageable. The Celtics had to trade Brown. The offers were far lower than we anticipated. Boston still managed to make the best of less-than-ideal circumstances and still factors prominently into the Eastern Conference championship picture.

Funnily enough, you could pretty easily argue that George would actually be a far better fit for this iteration of the 76ers than Brown is. Philadelphia's 20th-ranked offense has a bottom-five 3-point attempt rate and the eighth-highest average seconds per touch in the NBA. The Sixers could stand to trade some of that dribbling for a bit more shooting. Considering how lethal their transition offense can be, George's turnover generation would also fit this defense like a glove. The 76ers will get better offensively. We're still in tiny-sample season, and everyone's still learning how to play together. But George is undeniably the easier player to fit onto a roster like this than Brown.

Of course, the 76ers wouldn't have a roster like this without Brown. Widespread reporting has made it clear that Philadelphia's acquisition of Brown was what first caught the attention of LeBron James in free agency. If Brown was indeed a swing factor in the 76ers getting LeBron, that assuages any short-term salary concerns for Brown. For God's sake, the Philadelphia 76ers have LeBron James on a minimum contract. Even if Brown is overpaid, the surplus value on the James contract more than offsets any negative value there.

The 76ers have far less reason to fear an extension than Boston did as well. By trading Brown, the Celtics subjected him to the NBA's six-month extend-and-trade restrictions. That meant he could only tack one year onto his contract rather than two, and because he has multiple years remaining on his contract, he's not eligible to extend during the season. The 76ers therefore get to table those discussions until the offseason at the earliest, and remember, at that point, Brown will be negotiating off of the more modest statistics that come with sacrificing for the sake of a superteam. It's simply easier to envision Brown extending at less than the max in Philadelphia than it would have been in Boston.

Speaking of sacrificing, remember the whole "Jaylen Brown wants his own team" narrative from last offseason? For all we know, it was true at the time and might have remained true had he stayed with the Celtics. So far, that has been a complete non-issue for the 76ers. Brown is currently sporting his lowest usage rate since 2020 (before he became an All-Star). He's turning the ball over around half as often per 100 possessions as he did a season ago. He's an enormous part of a defense that surprisingly ranks No. 6 in the NBA so far this season. He's even openly called the 76ers Tyrese Maxey's team.

And the 76ers are, obviously, winning. They're mostly winning clutch games, but hey, you expect to win close games with four stars in your starting lineup. They're going to figure out the finer points of maximizing this talent mix over time, but even the "getting to know each other" version of this group poses almost impossible matchup problems for other teams. Take Cleveland, who has already faced Philadelphia twice. Can you guess which two Cavalier defenders have spent the most partial possessions guarding Brown, per NBA.com tracking data? James Harden and Donovan Mitchell, at 60.6 combined. Those are the sort of defenders you try to hide on weak scorers to preserve for offense. Well, where exactly are Harden and Mitchell supposed to hide against this team? There are no weak spots. The advantage of having this many creators is that Philadelphia basically starts every possession with an exploitable mismatch.

On pure talent accumulation alone, this is the sort of roster teams tend to go all-in for. Philadelphia didn't even have to. While the Stepien Rule complicates the tradability of some of their remaining picks, the 76ers are still slated to have four first-round picks in the next seven drafts. There is still ammunition for some sort of pivot here, whether that's a short-term upgrade to maximize this title run or more likely, some sort of long-term change at center as Joel Embiid gets older and potentially less reliable from a health perspective.

There are going to be depth questions down the line. Even if Brown gets less than a 35% max on his eventual extension, he's going to be pricey. Maxey feels like a near-lock for a supermax extension in the years to come, and while VJ Edgecombe will almost certainly be limited to 25% of the cap on his rookie extension, he'll still account for quite a bit of money. The 76ers are a top-heavy roster today, and that's after hitting a few home runs on the margins and getting arguably the greatest player of all time to take the minimum. Sustaining contention beyond the "Embiid is still a matchup nightmare and LeBron is on the team" era is going to require near-perfect management on the margins.

But this isn't rocket science. How many teams have a trio they can feel better about for, say, the next three-to-five years than Maxey, Brown and Edgecombe? The Brown trade opened an immediate championship window and likely ensured a relatively high baseline for the rest of the decade, assuming acceptable health and wise decisions elsewhere on the roster. It was a great trade in July and it remains a great trade today.
