#2514. U21 European Championship Final: English Manipulation of the German Pressing – MH

von Next Generation am 06.07.2025 in den Kategorien National Teams mit 1 Kommentar

England wins the U21 European Championship final against Germany 3-2. After just 20 minutes, England leads 2-0. This aspect analysis focuses on the reasons behind the German attacking press’s lack of access to England’s build-up play.

The U21 European Championship final offered several interesting tactical elements. This analysis focuses on Germany’s lack of access in their attacking pressing and marking. Particularly in the first half, England repeatedly managed to bypass the German press, often gaining large amounts of space in the final third, which led to dangerous scoring opportunities.

The early deficit also contributed to Germany being unable to focus, as they usually do, on securing depth in their pressing. Instead, they were forced to put direct pressure on the ball carrier in order to force turnovers. After the equalizer to make it 2-2, Germany noticeably pressed high less frequently. Therefore, this analysis examines Germany’s pressing and marking, as well as England’s build-up play, up to the 60th minute.

One of the trends at the U21 European Championship was that many teams aimed to press the opponent’s goal kicks with a +1 player on the last line or in the space between the lines just in front of the back line. Many teams—including Germany—used man-oriented marking when closing down during goal kicks.

Since most teams build up from a 1-4-2-4 structure on goal kicks, it is equally common to press man-to-man from a 4-1-3-2 shape, with the two holding midfielders (the “sixes”) staggered vertically.

The deeper-lying holding midfielder (for Germany: Martel) acts as the +1 player, positioning himself in space based on the location of the ball. When the opponent plays through the space between the lines, he can create a numerical advantage there. In the final third, pressing is carried out against a 1-4-2 build-up using a 3-2 shape. The more advanced holding midfielder (for Germany: Reitz) typically positions himself centrally and marks the ball-near holding midfielder, while the far-side winger presses the ball-far holding midfielder.

The English side, by contrast, caused problems for the German team’s marking assignments through an asymmetrical structure. As a result, England had several options for exploiting their numerical superiority in the build-up without having to immediately play into the space between the lines.

What remained consistent was the intention to establish central possession in front of the first pressing line using different players, in order to build up play on either side. Central possession makes it more difficult for the pressing team to steer the play in a specific direction, as the passing angles from central areas are wider than those from more advanced or wider positions.

Central possession complicates the opponent’s shaping of play. Anderson’s drop frees him from Woltemade’s marking shadow and creates a numerical advantage against Nebel, who must now cover both the advanced full-back and Anderson.

The asymmetry in England’s build-up play also allowed them to repeatedly exploit their numerical superiority in specific areas tailored to Germany’s pressing structure. By stretching the positioning of their two holding midfielders (the “sixes”), Reitz was forced to cover too much ground to mark both or to shift quickly to the ball-near midfielder.

Because Germany, for the reasons mentioned above, struggled to steer the press in a specific direction, Reitz was also unable to position himself closer to the ball-near player during goal kicks. Instead, he was forced to choose which of the two midfielders to mark man-to-man.

The wide, asymmetric positioning of the holding midfielders and advanced full-backs makes both midfielders available for passes, forcing Reitz to choose whom to mark. German forwards can’t shadow the opposing midfielders, while German wingers must decide between marking the spaced-out midfielders or full-backs.

England’s positional rotations during build-up play after goal kicks were most often initiated by holding midfielder Anderson. When Germany applied pressure (as shown in the diagram above), Anderson would frequently drop into the right half-space, almost into a right-sided centre-back position, while fellow holding midfielder Scott positioned himself more centrally, and No. 10 McAtee dropped into the higher left half-space.

When Anderson instead dropped centrally in front of the goalkeeper, the right centre-back would shift wide, which in turn affected the positioning of other central players and full-backs. The specific rotations of the key players, including their reference points and triggers, are discussed in more detail in the section on England’s build-up against Germany’s high pressing.

A key aspect of England’s build-up against Germany’s pressing was their ability to evade pressure through these rotations. Since Germany used man-oriented marking, they followed the English players during these movements, which repeatedly opened up spaces that England could then exploit. For example, when McAtee dropped deep into the far-side half-space, it pulled Martel—who was defending space-oriented in the center—out of position.

The aim was to repeatedly open up central areas by drawing German players out of the middle. When the full-backs, due to the rotations, were positioned deep and wide in possession, the ball-near holding midfielder would shift outward, thereby opening the central channel. This would often be followed by an overlapping run by the full-back into the half-space, allowing him to be found deep in the center with his marker behind him and plenty of space to operate.

Luring central players out of position and opening up space through rotations is one of the core principles of England’s build-up play. It significantly disrupted Germany’s ability to gain access through their man-marking approach during pressing.

Holding midfielder Anderson’s run outward opens the center, which can then be exploited by the full-back’s typical forward run.

England also added flexibility by repeatedly using long balls from their build-up play. Especially when both the full-backs and the holding midfielders were positioned deep, they opted for long passes as soon as Germany’s wingers and central players were lured far enough out. The 2–0 goal resulted from one such long ball, which was held up by striker Stansfield and laid off to the advancing Elliott and McAtee in the half-space, who now had plenty of room to operate in the open central area.

Although these long balls weren’t always as successful as in the lead-up to the 2–0, they had the effect of preventing Germany from pressing too aggressively, as players had to remain ready to cover depth in case of another long ball. For example, Martel pushed forward only hesitantly toward the dropping No. 10 McAtee, giving him significantly more time on the ball in central areas.

Against man-oriented marking systems, it is particularly important to apply intense pressure on the ball carrier, since progression is otherwise easier than against a zonal setup.

As described, England repeatedly managed to exploit their numerical advantage in the build-up. However, Germany’s pressing approach also contributed to their lack of access. The primary aim of Germany’s pressing when closing down is less about disrupting the build-up itself, and more about winning the ball in a way that immediately creates a transition opportunity.

To do so, Germany tries to use its forwards to immediately block passing lanes to the flanks, forcing the play through the third man or central passes.

Recovering possession through intercepting a pass has the advantage over winning a tackle in that it tends to allow better control of the ball and therefore more often leads to a transition opportunity. Additionally, central ball recoveries naturally result in a shorter route to goal and, statistically, in higher-quality chances in front of goal.

However, this type of pressing also means less pressure is placed on the ball carrier, since the focus is on directing play and winning the ball after a pass. As a result, England’s ball carriers had more time to locate the free +1 player, made available through asymmetry and rotations.

In hindsight, it might have been more effective to place greater emphasis on actively disrupting the build-up itself, because England repeatedly managed to bypass the German press dangerously. At the same time, Germany had the ability to control the game through their own possession, so it wasn’t absolutely necessary to rely on winning the ball high up the pitch to create chances.

Germany’s attacking pressing operated on principles similar to those of their closing down (Zustellen). From a 4-4-2 formation with a slightly advanced Reitz on the left half-space, the forwards aimed to channel the opponent’s build-up play out wide in order to isolate the wide build-up players and engage them in man-to-man marking.

On the last defensive line, Germany aimed to maintain a +1 numerical advantage, which is why the far-side holding midfielder was usually responsible for covering depth. The German wingers were expected to track back from the full-backs to press the half-backs in the three-man defensive line that frequently formed.

Even when applying attacking pressing from open play, Germany was rarely able to gain effective access to England’s build-up. This was primarily due to England’s positional play during build-up. England’s main objective in possession is to lure opponents out of position and then exploit the spaces that open up. This goal is achieved through positional rotations that make it especially difficult for the opponent to apply effective pressure on the ball carrier during pressing. The frequency of these rotations strongly resembles the rotation-heavy positional play famously associated with Paris Saint-Germain.

The following outlines the key running paths, rotations, and reference points of the most important players.

The center-backs were rarely involved in the rotations. Only when one of the holding midfielders dropped into the build-up line did the center-backs position themselves wider. Likewise, striker Stansfield provided a fixed presence in the central deep-lying position.

Most rotations initially originated from the holding midfielders, particularly Anderson. Most frequently, he dropped into the right half-space just ahead of the center-backs. This caused the right full-back to position wider and winger Elliott to drop deeper into the half-space at the level of the last defensive line. As a result, Woltemade and Nebel had to press two players, creating a 3 vs. 2 overload.

There were also occasions when Anderson dropped into the central center-back position. Consequently, the full-backs rotated into the half-spaces, or No. 10 McAtee dropped deeper. Notably, Anderson could be found almost anywhere on the pitch. At times, he overloaded the far side, which was then followed by a role swap between him and holding midfielder Scott.

Holding midfielder Scott often positioned himself in spaces that were left vacant after a sequence of rotations. Usually, Scott remained central or rotated roles with holding midfielder Anderson. It also happened that Scott took up an open full-back position when both the winger and the full-back rotated deep.

A particularly noticeable tendency of both holding midfielders was that, when in possession, they rotated toward the flank if a wide player was positioned close to the first build-up line, making themselves available along the sideline. This had the advantage of stretching the center even further.

This was especially important because England frequently won second balls after losing possession in build-up play. In the resulting transition situation, the central area was completely free, leading to several dangerous counter-attacks through the now open middle of the pitch.

Livramento, as the right full-back, primarily oriented himself around Anderson and the right winger Elliott. In relation to Elliott, Livramento always behaved in a complementary manner: when one occupied the wide position, the other took up the half-space. It was also common for Livramento to invert and drop into the deeper half-space, with Elliott moving wider in response, and vice versa.

Anderson served as a secondary reference point. Whenever Anderson dropped back to form a wide back three, Livramento either moved inverted or stayed wide and deep. If Anderson remained central, Livramento positioned himself near the center-backs in the half-space, from where he could rotate forward into depth if the outside lane was free.

On the left side, full-back Hinshelwood and winger Hutchinson rotated according to the same principles as Livramento and Elliott. Hinshelwood also frequently inverted into the deeper half-space or moved wide and deep. Both full-backs, Livramento and Hinshelwood, often initiated rotations through their inverted runs when the ball was with the near-side build-up player.

Runs into depth, however, were usually triggered only when other players moved to offer passing options. The No. 10 McAtee also played an important role as a reference point. When McAtee (and/or Hutchinson) moved into the left half-space, Hinshelwood rotated oppositely into depth.

McAtee, as a left-sided No. 10, had a freer role. He oriented himself around the holding midfielders to occupy or overload the central area when needed. He also rotated positions with left winger Hutchinson. Often, McAtee initially moved far into the left half-space to pull defenders out of the No. 10 zone behind him and then sometimes rotated further back toward the central center-back position.

In response, either full-back Hinshelwood or holding midfielder Anderson rotated forward into depth. Alternatively, winger Hutchinson could rotate into the half-space, prompting full-back Hinshelwood to rotate wider.

The English rotations created difficult conditions for Germany’s man-oriented attacking pressing. Man-marking was repeatedly manipulated, which in turn stretched and opened up spaces. Thanks to the flexibility of long balls and superiority in second balls, England’s build-up play additionally benefited in the first half. This led to repeated situations resembling counter-attacks, as England had plenty of central space available after bypassing the press.

The early goal also forced Germany to press higher more frequently and reduced their tendency to drop deep. Germany’s pressing behavior against England’s build-up thus became one of the decisive factors influencing the course of the game in the first half.

#2513. 2026 MLB Manager of the Year: White Sox's Will Venable, Brewers' Pat Murphy win BBWAA awards

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Chicago White Sox manager Will Venable and Brewers manager Pat Murphy were named the Managers of the Year in their respective leagues on Tuesday night as part of the BBWAA's awards week. Murphy is the first manager to ever win the award in three consecutive seasons.

The annual awards, which also include Manager of the Year, Reliever of the Year, Cy Young and MVP, are voted on by 30 members of the Baseball Writers Association of America (that's two per MLB city in each league). Votes were submitted before the beginning of the playoffs, meaning that only regular-season contributions are taken into account.

Murphy, manager of the World Series champion Milwaukee Brewers, has been voted the National League Manager of the Year, the Baseball Writers Association of America announced on Tuesday. He is the first person to win three consecutive Manager of the Year awards and the tenth person with three Manager of the Year wins in total.

Ballots for the BBWAA's awards are submitted between the end of the regular season and the beginning of the postseason. They are regular-season awards and Milwaukee's World Series win did not factor into the voting.

Of course, Murphy did not need the World Series win to boost his Manager of the Year case. He guided the small-market Brewers to baseball's best record (103-59) and run differential (+214) during the regular season, and their fourth consecutive NL Central title. Their 103 wins are a franchise record and baseball's most since 2023.

Murphy just completed his third season as Brewers manager and has three Manager of the Year wins to show for it. Bobby Cox (2004-05), Kevin Cash (2020-21), and Stephen Vogt (2024-25) are the only others with two consecutive Manager of the Year awards. Vogt was not an American League Manager of the Year finalist this season.

Prior to Murphy's threepeat here, the Brewers had never had a Manager of the Year winner. He's won the award now three times in three years at the helm.

Atlanta Braves manager Walt Weiss and Philadelphia Phillies manager Don Mattingly finished behind Murphy in the voting. Mattingly took over as an interim after the Phillies fired Rob Thomson on April 28. Philadelphia had baseball's fourth-best record after the managerial change. Weiss guided the Braves to the NL East title.

Venable, who helped orchestrate a 24-win year-to-year improvement and guided the team to its first postseason berth since 2021, has been named the American League Manager of the Year, the Baseball Writers Association of America announced on Tuesday. He beat out Tampa Bay Rays manager Kevin Cash and Boston Red Sox manager Chad Tracy.

The White Sox went 84-78 in 2026 after going 60-102 in 2025 and a hideous 41-121 in 2024. Those 121 losses are the record in baseball's Modern Era (since 1900). Venable's White Sox are the first team in history to reach the postseason after losing at least 100 games in the previous two seasons (they also lost 101 games in 2023).

The huge steps forward seem to be what secured the award for Venable. He took over in 2025 and the White Sox improved by 19 wins that season, only to turn around and improve by 24 more wins this past season. They were arguably the most surprising playoff team in 2026 and Venable gets his due here.

Venable joins the following White Sox manager of the year winners:

Cash finishes as the runner-up in a very close vote. Venable got 15 of the 30 first-place votes while Cash got 12. Tracy finishes in third place, with Guardians manager Stephen Vogt fourth and Yankees' skipper Aaron Boone sitting fifth.

Cash's Rays improved by 21 games to win an AL-best 98 and win the AL East after finishing in fourth place in 2025. Tracy took over the Red Sox after Alex Cora started 10-17 and was fired. Tracy went 77-58 and earned the second AL wild card.

#2512. NFL pretenders and contenders after Week 9: NFC North is fierce, no faith in Giants and Steelers

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Now that we are halfway through the 2026 NFL season, it's time to start paying attention to the playoff picture -- and it's a pretty wild picture to look at right now.

The NFC North is the only division to ever feature four teams three or more games above .500 through Week 9, while the NFC South is the only division to feature four teams two or more games below .500. Is every NFC North team going to make the playoffs? And which NFC South team will likely go one-and-done in the postseason?

Below, we will break down the pretenders and contenders in the NFL right now. We will look at the 14 teams that would make the playoffs if the season ended today, and examine if they have a legitimate shot to hoist the Lombardi Trophy. Let's begin with the contenders.

The 7-1 Buffalo Bills are off to their best eight-game start to a season since 1993, which was when they made their last Super Bowl appearance. Josh Allen is again an MVP favorite, James Cook has rushed for at least 75 yards and a touchdown in seven straight games, and Jim Leonhard's defense left the Minnesota Vikings front office scrambling after Carson Wentz registered one of the worst quarterback showings in franchise history on Monday night. The Bills are again a contender.

The San Francisco 49ers are your Super Bowl favorites right now over at DraftKings Sportsbook (+540), and it's easy to understand why. They have started 7-1 or better for the first time since 2019, when they made the Super Bowl. Brock Purdy is an MVP favorite, and he leads an offense that is averaging 29.4 points per game -- which ranks No. 3 in the NFL. This past week against the Las Vegas Raiders, the 49ers scored two passing touchdowns, two rushing touchdowns and a defensive touchdown. However, health will again be a major talking point when it comes to San Francisco. Wide receivers Mike Evans and Deebo Samuel are still sidelined, and defensive tackle Gracen Halton suffered a broken ankle on Sunday. If they can return some players for the stretch run, this could be the 49ers' year.

The Denver Broncos have been dancing with the devil all season in these one-score games, but I'll remind you Bo Nix and Co. did the same thing last year, and probably would have made the Super Bowl if Nix didn't suffer that ankle injury in the divisional round. The Broncos have won five straight games since their 2-2 start, and while they have the worst yard differential (-699) by any team that started 7-2 or better in NFL history, all Nix has done is step up in crunch time. He's 18-12 in his career when trailing in the second half, and 13-12 when trailing in the fourth quarter. Those are the best win percentages by any quarterback since 1970, with a minimum of 20 games. Defensively, Denver is giving up more yards per game than last year, but still ranks top 10 in scoring with 20.7 points allowed per game. You could make the case that the Broncos are pretenders, but I'm leaning the other way. They beat Josh Allen and the Bills in the playoffs last year, and have already defeated the Jacksonville Jaguars and Kansas City Chiefs this season. Denver could make the AFC Championship again.

The Jaguars are all-in this year. At the trade deadline, they sent a first-round pick, second-round pick, a future second-round pick, a future fifth-round pick and a conditional sixth-round pick for defensive tackle Jordan Davis, defensive tackle Davon Godchaux and safety Jessie Bates III. Giving up first- and second-round picks for Davis was shocking, but there's no doubt the Jaguars roster got better this week.

The Jags are running away with the AFC South at 6-2, and have as many wins as the rest of their rivals combined. They are 14-2 in their past 16 games dating back to last year, and Trevor Lawrence has statistically been the best quarterback during that stretch with 42 total touchdowns and a 108.8 passer rating. The Jaguars have the second-best scoring defense in the NFL (15.1 points allowed per game) and one of the best run defenses in the league as well, allowing just 89.3 yards per game. Justice Hill actually just became the first running back to rush for 75 yards against the Jags in 25 games.

The Chiefs got back on track this past week against the New York Jets, registering their largest win (23 points) since Week 7 in 2025. Kenneth Walker III also got back on track with 143 total yards and three touchdowns. There's still some concern around Patrick Mahomes' passing game, but the addition of Josh Downs will be helpful. Chiefs receivers are averaging 117.5 yards per game, which ranks 28th in the NFL. That hasn't stopped Kansas City from having what is statistically the second-best offense in the NFL (384.1 yards per game).

This may be Joe Burrow's year to win MVP. He's accounted for 26 total touchdowns through eight games. Five of the previous seven players to score that many touchdowns through eight games won MVP. Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins have combined for 47 receptions, 693 yards and eight touchdowns just over the last three games. We know what Chase is capable of, but Higgins is having the best year of his NFL career. He's averaging 94.8 receiving yards per game and has caught six touchdowns in eight games.

Where there's concern with the Cincinnati Bengals is their rushing attack. The 85.6 rushing yards per game are the fewest by a team to start 6-2 or better since the 2014 Detroit Lions. We'll see if the Bengals can pass their way to a Super Bowl. Cincy's defense still isn't "great" statistically, but it's much improved compared to the past couple of seasons. That in itself gives the Bengals a legitimate shot.

It's hard not to like the Chicago Bears. They have an offensive madman scheming up talented weapons open downfield, a quarterback who looks like Josh Allen, and a defense that has been sparked by the addition of Jeffery Simmons. The Bears can't turn the ball over five times every game as they did on Sunday night, but I'm not too worried about that issue.

The Bears have the firepower offensively to be a Super Bowl contender, from the rushing attack to the passing attack, and a defense that is good enough to support a playoff run. The addition of Simmons affects that unit in more ways than one. He can stuff the run and can pressure the quarterback from the interior -- which in turn makes life easier on those in the secondary.

I'm on the fence with the Lions. We all know about the offense with Jared Goff, Jahmyr Gibbs and Amon-Ra St. Brown, but the issue has always been Detroit's defense.

The reason I'll place the Lions in the "contender" category is that Kelvin Sheppard's unit has been better in recent weeks. After a disastrous start, the Lions have allowed just 15.5 points per game during this current four-game win streak. They were allowing 31.8 points per game during the 2-2 start. With Brian Branch back, hopefully Kerby Joseph soon, and the addition of Andre Cisco, I think the Lions can be a contender.

If I were power-ranking the teams in the NFC North, I would have the Green Bay Packers third or fourth. So, does that make them a contender or pretender? I'm still trying to figure that out.

The turnaround in Green Bay has been incredible. After that horrific 1-2 start, the Packers are playing better on both sides of the ball. Jordan Love is the best deep-ball thrower in the NFL, and Christian Watson and Matthew Golden are looking like Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle did in Miami during those fun Mike McDaniel years. The two have combined for 1,662 receiving yards thus far. However, like the Bengals, the Packers can't run the ball. They rank dead last in rushing offense with 68.2 yards per game, and just lost Josh Jacobs to a broken finger.

I'm not placing money on the Packers to win the Super Bowl, but I can't get over how good this passing attack has been. Plus, the defense just picked off Drake Maye three times and will return Micah Parsons soon.

The Vikings were perhaps the most obvious pretender in the NFL despite the 6-2 record. Kyler Murray's passing offense was statistically one of the worst in the NFL, as his 170.3 passing yards per game ranked 30th among 31 qualifying passers entering Week 9. When Carson Wentz replaced him in the lineup on Monday night against Buffalo, some people thought it would open up the offense a bit. Instead, Wentz registered the worst passer rating by a Vikings quarterback (8.9) in a game since 1984, while completing 32% of his passes.

However, I'm willing to entertain the possibility that the Vikings are now contenders with the addition of Kirk Cousins at the trade deadline. He's been playing good football for the Raiders, as his 20 passing touchdowns rank second in the NFL, and his 260.0 passing yards per game rank eighth. Cousins has chemistry with Justin Jefferson -- and that may be an understatement. Jefferson's 98.9 receiving yards per game when catching passes from Cousins are the most by a QB-WR duo all-time (min. 50 games). With the backing of a Brian Flores defense, the Vikings are a team to watch moving forward.

The New York Giants are the frontrunner in the NFC East, but I don't know how realistic their Super Bowl chances are. In fact, DraftKings Sportsbook believes the 3-5 Houston Texans and 3-6 Tampa Bay Buccaneers have just as good a shot at winning it all this year.

J.J. McCarthy has been better than expected at the quarterback position, but still hasn't thrown a touchdown in his two starts. In fact, he's the only quarterback in the past 40 years to win a game with zero passing touchdowns in four straight starts. New York has what is statistically a top five defense under new coordinator Dennard Wilson and Defensive Rookie of the Year favorite Arvell Reese, but there are at least five teams in the NFC I'm more confident in.

The New England Patriots were destroyed at home by the Packers on Sunday, 45-27. Those 45 points were the most allowed in a home game since 1970. Christian Gonzalez struggled to keep up with the dynamic duo of Christian Watson and Matthew Golden, while Drake Maye threw three interceptions. To make matters worse, running back Rhamondre Stevenson is reportedly dealing with a knee injury that will sideline him for a couple of weeks, while TreVeyon Henderson remains out after experiencing an "unusual medical emergency." The Patriots running backs are now Corey Kiner and Lan Larison.

Even with Mike Tomlin gone, I still view the Pittsburgh Steelers the same. A feisty team that can make the playoffs and maybe even steal the division, but is not a legitimate Super Bowl contender.

With that said, there are reasons to believe the Steelers could be a sleeper. Aaron Rodgers' offense is averaging 26.2 points per game over their last six, plus Jaylen Warren is one of the most improved players in the NFL this season. He's already up to 998 total yards in eight games played. That ranks fifth in the NFL.

Whether the Carolina Panthers win the NFC South or not, I don't view them as a Super Bowl contender. The Panthers have lost three straight games and are averaging 17.7 points per contest during this skid. Carolina's offensive line and cornerback room have been hit hard by injuries, and this team is now a +225 underdog to win the division.

#2511. Vincent Kompany returns to Bayern Munich training ground after illness

Bayern Munich head coach Vincent Kompany was reportedly back at the club's training ground at Säbener Straße on Tuesday after being absent due to illness since collapsing on October 23.

According to TZ, Kompany was sitting at his computer in his office at the club's headquarters shortly after 10am.

The 40-year-old Belgian coach was greeted by assistant Floribert Ngalula and later held a longer conversation with sporting director Christoph Freund.

From his office, Kompany was also able to watch injured players such as Luis Diaz and Jamal Musiala continue their rehabilitation training on the pitch.

Kompany had been absent since collapsing on the training pitch on October 23, two days before Bayern Munich's 3-1 Bundesliga win over SC Freiburg.

The 40-year-old was subsequently diagnosed with meningeal irritation and continued his recovery at home after being discharged from hospital.

Bayern assistant Aaron Danks was in charge for the five games Kompany missed.

Kompany is expected to return to the touchline when Bayern Munich face 1. FC Köln in the Bundesliga on November 20, following the international break.

#2509. Ranking NFL's greatest in-season trades of all-time: Where Kirk Cousins to Vikings ranks among top 10

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

While it was quiet for a while, there were plenty of fireworks during the final hours of Tuesday's NFL trade deadline. The biggest trade was the one that sent quarterback Kirk Cousins back to Minnesota.

As it currently stands, that is already one of the most notable in-season trades in NFL history. Quarterbacks of Cousins' stature are almost never traded during a season, especially not to a team that is in position to possibly win a division title. Making this trade even more notable is that the Raiders, who received a third-round pick in exchange for Cousins, will now give the keys to the offense to No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza.

Here's where the Cousins trade already ranks among the biggest in-season deals of all time.

The 1981 Chargers were involved in seismic trades, two of which included receivers. The first sent All-Pro John Jefferson to the Packers in a blockbuster trade that included a 1983 first-round pick and second-round picks in 1982 and 1984.

Two weeks after trading Jefferson, the Chargers traded for then-Saints receiver Wes Chandler, who provided an immediate spark for the "Air Coryell" offense. Chandler helped the Chargers advance to that year's AFC title game. He had 12 catches in two playoff games along with a big punt return for a score in the Chargers' overtime win over the Dolphins in the divisional round.

Chandler led the NFL in receiving yards and touchdown catches the following season and was named to the Pro Bowl three times during his first four seasons in San Diego. Jefferson, however, never again matched the level of success he had with the Chargers.

Wes Chandler 8️⃣9️⃣ pic.twitter.com/bYEvNBFbN9

Tuesday's trade has a chance to be one of the most consequential in NFL history. The trade officially signaled the beginning of the Mendoza era in Las Vegas, and it also infused life into a 6-2 Vikings team that desperately needed help at quarterback.

Tuesday's trade represented a full-circle moment for Cousins, who never wanted to leave Minnesota in the first place. After a two-plus year hiatus, Cousins will get another chance to lead the Vikings on a possible playoff run.

Rams GM Les Snead's "F them picks" philosophy eventually led to a Super Bowl win for the Rams. The trade for Ramsey two years earlier helped make that championship possible.

The Rams gave the Jaguars a first-round selection in the 2020 NFL Draft in addition to first- and fourth- round picks in the 2021 draft for Ramsey, who in 2017 had led the Jaguars within a game of the Super Bowl. Ramsey was named to the Pro Bowl during his first four seasons with the Rams. He had four picks, 16 pass breakups, a forced fumble and a fumble recovery during the Rams' Super Bowl-winning season.

After a 6-10 outfit in 1980, the 49ers were off to a 3-2 start in 1981 when they sent first- and second-round picks in the 1983 NFL Draft to the Chargers in exchange for Dean. Dean was a Pro Bowler each of the previous two years and also mired in a contract dispute.

Just days after coming to San Francisco, Dean had a pair of sacks while helping the 49ers record a 45-14 win over the Cowboys, the same team the 49ers would later defeat in the NFC title game. With the 49ers, Dean recorded 12 sacks in 11 games that season while helping San Francisco win their first Super Bowl. Dean helped San Francisco win another Super Bowl in 1984 before being inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2008.

#49ers greats Randy Cross and Ronnie Lott discuss the legend of Fred Dean. 🚬"James Dean wasn't cooler than Fred Dean."Dean made his #FTTB debut, 43 years ago today — arguably the greatest mid-season acquisition in NFL history.October 11, 1981 pic.twitter.com/jYXDDsTYaK

Bobby Layne was Detroit royalty ... until he wasn't. Five years after leading the Lions to back-to-back NFL titles, Layne was traded to the Steelers just two weeks into the 1958 season. A year earlier, the Lions won their third title with Tobin Rote at quarterback after Layne broke his leg during the second-to-last game of the regular season.

At the time of the trade, Layne allegedly said that the Lions would not win for another 50 years, a statement that became known as the "Bobby Lane Curse." Detroit is still trying to win its first title since 1957.

Layne, who was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1967, played five seasons for the Steelers, earning two Pro Bowls over that span and posting a 27-19-2 record as the team's starting quarterback. He said in his autobiography that his biggest career regret was not winning a title in Pittsburgh.

In Week 5 of the 1983 season, the Raiders suffered their first loss after a 38-37 shootout to Washington, the defending Super Bowl champs who set the NFL single-season scoring record. Al Davis, the Raiders owner and general manager, responded by aggressively pursuing Mike Haynes, who was stuck in a contentious holdout with the Patriots.

While Davis offered Haynes a way out of his situation, Haynes acknowledged decades later that joining the Raiders wasn't an easy decision.

"I actually didn't like the Raiders at all," Haynes told CBS Sports in a 2020 interview. "I didn't like any other team except the Patriots. When Al Davis called, I actually had to think about it. The Raiders were the team where one of my teammates [receiver Darryl Stingley] was paralyzed. I had to think about all that. But I justified it because they had just moved from Oakland to L.A. I grew up in Los Angeles … In my head, I needed to do that to be open to going there. I told Mr. Davis I'd love to go there."

It ended up being a perfect fit for both parties. Haynes teamed up with Lester Hayes to form one of the best cornerback duos in NFL history. The duo shut down Hall of Fame receiver Steve Largent in the AFC title game, and in Super Bowl XVIII, they helped hold Washington's explosive offense to just nine points. The Raiders' 38-9 win remains one of the most surprising outcomes in Super Bowl history.

Haynes played six more seasons with the Raiders, earning three Pro Bowls over that span. He was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1997. The Patriots, who received a 1984 first-round pick and a 1985 second-round pick, reached the Super Bowl in 1985. Irving Fryer, who was drafted using the 1984 first-round pick, played a key role in the Patriots' first AFC title.

Despite rushing for over 1,000 yards in each of his first two seasons, Lynch was found to be expendable by the Bills midway through the 2010 season. Before the deadline, Buffalo traded Lynch to Seattle in exchange for a 2011 fourth-round pick and a 2012 fifth-round pick.

Simply put, Lynch and the Seahawks were the perfect fit. After running over the defending champion Saints in the 2010 wild card round, Lynch earned Pro Bowl honors in each of his first four full seasons in Seattle.

He was among Seattle's key figures during the team's Super Bowl run in 2013 and NFC Championship run in 2014. In six seasons with the Seahawks, Lynch rushed for 6,347 yards and 79 touchdowns during the regular season, plus 937 yards and nine scores in 11 postseason games.

McCaffrey was dealt to the 49ers in a blockbuster deal that landed the Panthers 2023 second-, third- and fourth-round picks, plus a fifth-rounder in 2024. The trade ended a six-year run in Carolina for McCaffrey, who was selected No. 8 overall in the 2017 NFL Draft.

The deal paid immediate dividends for both McCaffrey and the 49ers, who were 3-3 at the time of the trade. San Francisco reached the NFC title game that year before injuries proved too much to overcome. In 2023, however, the 49ers reached the Super Bowl behind a banner year from McCaffrey, who won his first rushing title that season. San Francisco had the lead in overtime in that year's Super Bowl before falling victim to Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes.

McCaffrey has remained a highly productive player for the 49ers. This past Sunday, he broke Marshall Faulk's record for the most career touchdown receptions (37) for a running back in the Super Bowl era.

The Rams and Colts stunned the NFL when Indianapolis traded two players, three first-round picks and three second-round picks to Los Angeles in exchange for Dickerson, the league's reigning Offensive Player of the Year. In 1984, he became the first player in NFL history to rush for over 2,100 yards in a season.

Dickerson led the Colts to the playoffs in 1987, their first playoff appearance since the franchise moved from Baltimore to Indianapolis in 1984. The following season, Dickerson led the NFL in rushing, then rushed for over 1,311 yards in 1989.

Happy Halloween #Colts fans! 🎃Here's a look back on this day in 1988 when Eric Dickerson showed up as Superman: pic.twitter.com/zGhWzaQUta

The Rams, despite losing Dickerson, would make the playoffs in each of the next three seasons, which included a trip to the NFC Championship Game in 1989.

The Buffalo Bills were also part of this trade, giving up several assets that included future high picks in exchange for future All-Pro linebacker Cornelius Bennett, who would help the Bills become the first team in NFL history to appear in four consecutive Super Bowls during the 1990s.

"I find out that we had just traded the only guy on our team that was really any good. And I couldn't believe it."

Troy Aikman, needless to say, wasn't thrilled upon hearing the news that the Dallas Cowboys and new head coach Jimmy Johnson had traded their best player, running back Herschel Walker, to the Minnesota Vikings in exchange for a bounty of future draft picks. Walker, a former Heisman Trophy winner and 1,500-yard back the previous season, was leaving a team that would ultimately go 1-15 during Johnson's first season in Dallas. While the trade was widely unpopular at the time, Johnson was confident that it was the right thing to do.

"One agent said it's the biggest trade he has ever seen in the NFL," Johnson said during a press conference following the trade, "and one owner said it's a great train robbery. Whatever it is, we're happy with it."

The Cowboys used the picks to help build what would become one of the best rosters in NFL history. In 1990, they used their first pick from the trade to select Emmitt Smith, who would go on to become the NFL's all-time leading rusher. Over the following two drafts, the Cowboys selected future Pro Bowl defensive tackle Russell Maryland, perennial starting cornerback Kevin Smith, and future three-time All-Pro safety Darren Woodson.

A blockbuster trade that sparked the beginning of a dynasty.29 years ago today, the Vikings acquired RB Herschel Walker... And the rest is history for the @dallascowboys. #TDIH #FBF (via @nflthrowback) pic.twitter.com/UG8gHsgehr

Along with several other acquisitions, the Cowboys went from NFL doormats to NFL champions. In 1992, just three years after pulling off the greatest deadline deal in league history, Dallas won the first of its three Super Bowls over four years.

"I couldn't understand it at the time, but I'm glad they viewed it differently," Aikman said during an interview with NFL Films. "It certainly got us over the hump in a hurry."

#2508. Celtics vs. 76ers winners and losers: Jayson Tatum outduels Jaylen Brown, but Paul George steals the show

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Nick Nurse nailed it. A lot of people had a lot to say in advance of the Celtics and 76ers facing each other for the first time this season, but Philadelphia's coach summed it up pretty well before the two teams tipped off on Tuesday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

"This is probably one -- maybe the one -- that people were circling in the summertime when the schedule came out," Nurse said.

Nick Nurse on his morning conversation with Jaylen Brown and hype surrounding the grudge match with the Celtics.“This is probably one — maybe the one — that people were circling in the summer time when the schedule came out. It’s finally here.” pic.twitter.com/CdBoE576iI

He wasn't kidding. From the moment Jaylen Brown was traded to the Sixers, the hype and drama surrounding the first meeting between him and his old team -- and his longtime running mate-turned-rival, Jayson Tatum -- have been seemingly endless. While Tatum tried to lower the heat on the simmering feud, claiming that he was "caught off guard as much as the rest of the world" when Brown was shipped to Philly, Brown was all too happy to add rhetorical fuel to the fire, saying there might not be beef between the two players, but there was some "lamb chops and gravy" and warning his former teammate to "stay ready at all times."

By Tuesday, there wasn't much left unsaid. When Brown was asked whether he would talk to Tatum prior to the game, he dismissed the idea: "There's nothing to talk about. He's on his side, I'm on my side. We're playing basketball. Both of us are trying to win. So there's nothing to talk about. Check the ball up."

The old saying about being careful what you wish for comes to mind. They checked the ball up and the Celtics ran the Sixers off their floor in what ended up as a blowout 123-101 win for Boston. Aside from the actual victory for the Celtics that moved them ahead of the Sixers in the standings and into first place in the Eastern Conference, here are the winners and losers from the most anticipated game of the season to date, including the under-discussed player in the Brown-to-Philly deal having the performance of the night.

The Sixers beating the Celtics in the first round of the playoffs last year was the outlier, not the rule. Boston tends to get the better of Philly in big games. Tatum and the Celtics reminded everyone about that on Tuesday. He finished with 21 points, six rebounds, four assists and two blocks. And a whole lot of bragging rights.

We got some Tatum vs. Brown one-on-one matchups early, with Tatum getting the better of the duel at the defensive end.

Jayson Tatum forces the turnover on Jaylen Brown in their first iso of the game.📺 NBA on NBC and Peacock pic.twitter.com/IOStW8Kk93

And while his most memorable play didn't come against Brown, Tatum still had the highlight of the evening when he threw down a monster dunk on LeBron James.

JAYSON TATUM WITH THE POSTER ON LEBRON JAMES!📺 NBA on NBC and Peacock pic.twitter.com/LOXzzT0FjJ

Brown was right. There wasn't anything left to talk about. Tatum did his talking on the court.

This was always going to be a zero-sum game. Tatum won, Brown lost. But the way Brown went down wasn't great as far as optics and narratives go. He was held to a season-low 13 points, got in foul trouble, had four turnovers and was a game-worst minus-27. Oof.

Apart from a nice dunk in the first half, it was a game for Brown to forget. Making matters worse, the guy he got traded for had a night to remember.

"I'm a bit frustrated, honestly," Brown said after the game. "I wanted to perform better for my team. Foul trouble kind of derailed me a little bit, but it happens. It's unfortunate, but now we got to just move on to the next."

When the Sixers traded George, it seemed like a magic trick by new president of basketball operations Mike Gansey. George played just 78 largely unspectacular games over two seasons in Philly. Beyond that, he's six years older than Brown and still had two years and more than $110 million left on his deal.

So naturally, George has looked like the best version of himself since leaving Philly and going to Boston. His hot start to the season continued on Tuesday with him dropping 36 points on 14 for 22 shooting from the field, including making six of his 11 3-point attempts. He was so good against his former team that at one point he inspired NBC's Noah Eagle on the play-by-play call to exclaim, "PG-13 has turned Rated R." (Prepackaged, but still a great line.)

PAUL GEORGE HAS 30 POINTSVINTAGE PG. 🔥🔥🔥 pic.twitter.com/AH8RI4yVnp

It was supposed to be either Tatum or Brown's night, but George ended up commanding the biggest spotlight with how well he played. He also got the last laugh after an interaction with a Philly fan who, according to George, "dropped the ball on the ground like I'm a dog to go fetch or go get it instead of passing the ball to me like a normal fan." In response, George said he "rolled him a middle finger."

Looks like Paul George may have also flipped out a fan (or someone) after that three pic.twitter.com/LecXldKldE

With Brad Stevens in the front office and Joe Mazzulla on the sideline, the Celtics have long had a theory of the case: Take more 3s than their opponents and bet that they'll make more. That gamble has served them well more often than not. They won a championship that way while leading the league in 3-point attempts and makes per game during the 2023-24 season. The strategy did not work as well against the Sixers in the last postseason, but the Celtics have made peace with the approach, win or lose.

Nothing has changed. Boston still loves to fire away from deep, and that's exactly what the Celtics did against the Sixers on Tuesday. Boston shot 45% from beyond the arc (22 for 49), compared to just 30% for Philadelphia (11 for 37).

When the outside shots are falling for the Celtics, they're tough to beat. No one knows that better than Jaylen Brown.

Why shake hands or hug when you can just turn your back and offer a cold shoulder instead?

The pregame moment between Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown.📺 NBA on NBC and Peacock pic.twitter.com/P4iclUnqZ5

When asked about this moment, Brown told reporters he "wasn't paying attention" when Tatum attempted to greet him.

"I'm just focused on coming out and doing what's best for my team. Everything else was just, to be honest, I wasn't paying attention," Brown said. "Credit to Jayson, he played well tonight. Credit to the Celtics, they executed, they shot the hell out of the ball and were the better team tonight."

Arguably the best part of Brown ignoring Tatum was Tatum then immediately going to LeBron James for an intricate handshake and embrace right afterward.

Looks like Jayson Tatum tried to dap up/hug Jaylen Brown but it wasn’t reciprocated pic.twitter.com/6iMOrpvmmD

Pretty much everyone was asked about Tatum and Brown, from Joe Mazzulla talking about how the trade could have been handled differently, to Payton Pritchard weighing in on whether there was beef between them, to Paul George taking credit for helping the Sixers "land a future piece" in Brown by getting traded (all the lols there).

The winner, though, was 76ers guard Kentavious Caldwell-Pope, who, unlike Pritchard, didn't try to minimize the suspected animosity between Tatum and Brown -- or at least what appears to be some obvious hurt feelings from Brown's side. When Caldwell-Pope was asked about the situation, he pointed to a social media interaction as proof of what we all suspected anyway.

"I don't know what the tension was before JB left," Caldwell-Pope said. "All I know is when he wrote on the comments when JT did that little interview, that's all I know. That's all I need to know."

Kentavious Caldwell-Pope says Jaylen Brown mindset going into the matchup with the Celtics is he’s trying to BTA:“I don’t know what the tension was before but before JB left all I know is when he wrote on the comments when JT did that little interview, that’s all I know, that’s… pic.twitter.com/Co8Wkh0APS

If you somehow missed it, "that little interview" was Tatum claiming that he found out about the trade when everyone else did -- which prompted Brown to pop up in the comments with a cap emoji, essentially calling Tatum a liar. Credit to Caldwell-Pope for calling it like it is rather than pretending.

Speaking of pretending, Nurse was asked about how Brown was approaching the game and reached into his bag of coach clichés for a classic favored by so many in his profession during times like these.

"He's approaching it as another game," Nurse said. "Big game. He's excited for the opportunity, but he wasn't expressing it in a personal way. He said this is a really good test for our team, and I agree with him."

Nick Nurse on how Jaylen Brown is approaching tonight’s game:“He's approaching it as another game. Big game. He's excited for the opportunity, but he wasn't expressing it in a personal way. He said this is a really good test for our team, and I agree with him.” pic.twitter.com/6MiBQXBVCx

Brown advised Tatum to stay ready at all times and everyone from the fans to the media dined out on the pork chops and gravy remarks for weeks in advance. It's hard to sell that as just another game.

Full marks to whoever came up with the song selection for Celtics shootaround on Tuesday.

Celtics shootaround underway with “why can’t we be friends” playing. pic.twitter.com/EJV3A8pQKL

Not long before tip-off, ESPN's Shams Charania reported that Tatum and Brown had a "heart-to-heart" in France prior to the trade. According to the report, the meeting occurred shortly after Brown was dangled in a failed trade attempt for Giannis Antetokounmpo, but before he was sent to Philadelphia.

That sounded pretty juicy, except to hear longtime NBA guard Evan Turner tell it on social media, "this didn't happen." Not to be outdone, Carmelo Anthony also weighed in on the topic, saying that being around the two in France was "weird."

Carmelo Anthony says the energy was weird with Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown in France when they we're all together just days before the trade happened pic.twitter.com/NQ0rGnt5Vh

Turner's source on the subject was unclear, but he was pretty emphatic about the denial, insisting in the comments to the story that the pair never spoke. Not sure that anyone predicted Turner coming off the top rope to smack down an NBA report, but if this ends with him or Carmelo becoming the new Woj, we're all in for a treat.

#2507. Prisco's Week 10 NFL picks: Giants over Commanders on 'TNF,' Lions top Patriots in Munich

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

A perfect week. Can you believe it? I went 15-0 with my straight-up picks last week. I guess it was an easy week, like some said.

As for my picks against the spread, it wasn't quite as good, but it was better than it's been. I went 9-6 for the week, which I will take.

The season marks are now 59-74-3 ATS and 87-48-1 straight up. Let's see if we can get perfect against the spread this week.

Yeah, right. I will take three games above. 500 again as I make the climb to respectability.

The Giants are back home after beating the Eagles and now face a Commanders team that probably has to win this to have any chance at the playoffs. The Giants' defense has been dominant up front as of late, and that will continue here as they contain Jayden Daniels. Giants keep winning.

This is a big game for both teams, but especially so for the Patriots after they got blown out by the Packers at home last week. The Lions won at Miami and didn't play great, but they will get it going on offense here. New England is struggling on defense, so look for the Lions to win it with a strong offensive showing.

The Chiefs snapped a two-game losing streak last week in beating the Jets, while the Falcons were blown out in Madrid by the Bengals. The defense had some major issues in that game. That will be the same here after the trade of safety Jessie Bates. Chiefs stack another victory.

This is a big game for both teams in terms of the playoff picture. The Texans looked dominant against the Chargers last week, but this is a second straight road game. It won't matter. Their defensive front will dominate whoever plays quarterback for the Browns. But the Cleveland defense will keep them in it.

The Packers are coming off an impressive road victory over the Patriots and Jordan Love has been on fire. But the Minnesota defense is special and now they have Kirk Cousins to play quarterback. Even so, look for the Packers to win another one as their defense limits Cousins and the offense.

The Titans are coming off a bye, while the Jaguars are coming off a victory last Thursday at Baltimore. They will be rested too. Jacksonville is riding high as one of the top teams in the league and made some moves at the trade deadline to get even better. Though this is a rivalry, with some unpredictable games, this won't be. Jaguars big.

This is the dog game of the week between two struggling teams. But one is young and playing hard on the way up, while one is on the way down after trading away assets. The problem for Miami is that quarterback Malik Willis is out. That means Kyle McCord will start at quarterback. Miami will hang around against the depleted Colts team, but the Colts will win it late.

This is an enormous game in the division, even though both teams have just three victories. The winner will be in first place. The Saints beat the Browns last week, while the Panthers have lost three straight. The Saints make it four in a row as Tyler Shough has a big day.

The Bills are coming off a hard-fought road victory at Minnesota. The turnaround will be tough, but they are playing at a high level. The defense is improving. Look for Josh Allen to carve up the Jets' defense.

The Seahawks will start Drew Lock at quarterback again in this one. He was just OK last week against Arizona. But the Raiders have big-time defensive issues. For the Raiders, it's Fernando Mendoza time after they traded Kirk Cousins to Minnesota. This is a tough defense for a first NFL start. Look for Lock to win it as the Seahawks' defense does the rest.

The Rams lost at home to the Cardinals a few weeks ago and now must play without Puka Nacua. How will they move the ball? The Cardinals will start rookie Carson Beck at quarterback. Going against Myles Garrett and company can be a problem. Rams win it, but it's low-scoring.

The Cowboys can't afford another loss in their division race, so this is a huge game for them. The 49ers are riding high and that offense will challenge the Dallas defense. But I think the Dallas offense will be even better. Upset special. Dak Prescott has a bigger day than Brock Purdy.

This is for first place in the division. The Bengals are riding high behind their passing game and Joe Burrow. But the defense can't stop the run. The Steelers will run it here to keep Burrow off the field. It doesn't work. The Bengals will once again win it behind Burrow and the passing game.

This game had promise before the season, but the Ravens are without Lamar Jackson and the Chargers are 0-8. Jacoby Brissett will start for the Ravens, which should help the offense some. The Chargers have struggled on offense, but I think their defense will keep them in this. It's close.

#2506. Kirk Cousins' reunion with Vikings headlines NFL trade deadline; Georgia tops CFP Top 25 rankings

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This is an article version of the CBS Sports HQ AM Newsletter, the ultimate guide to every day in sports. You can sign up to get it in your inbox every weekday morning here.

The trade deadline is all about the deals that actually get done, but what about the ones that never cross the finish line? The Bengals learned a hard lesson about the compensatory pick formula on Tuesday and called off a trade because of it. They were in agreement with the Eagles on a swap that would send Arnold Ebiketie to Cincinnati in return for a 2027 sixth-round pick but backed out when they realized the ramifications. Our Jordan Dajani explained the bizarre situation when he labeled the Bengals as the deadline's biggest losers.

That's an example of what not to do if you're inside an NFL front office. But as we shift our focus back to the trades that did come to fruition, we have to recognize the masterclass the 49ers put on. They landed Keenan Allen on Tuesday to add to a haul that already included DeForest Buckner. In securing much-needed wide receiver help, they became one of four teams to receive an "A" grade on our trade deadline report card. For context, here's a look at the rest of the NFC West:

Defensive players are important, too! In fact, many of the splashiest moves included defensive linemen and defensive backs. Take Amani Hooker, for instance. The Bills gave up a second-round pick to land the NFL's interception leader in one of the top five deals of the deadline.

It's hard to say that any team got better than the Jaguars (they made three splashes and boosted an already prolific defense), but the Chiefs also upgraded significantly. Josh Downs is the newest member of their wide receiver group by way of a win-win trade with the Colts.

Pete Prisco finalized his latest set of NFL Power Rankings before the last-minute hustle of trade deadline moves, so the dip the Vikings took ahead of Week 10 emphasizes just how important it was for them to add Kirk Cousins. Minnesota was the biggest faller of the week, down five spots to No. 11. Most teams' trades (or lack thereof) were already factored into the equation, though, so it should not come as a surprise to see the deadline's most active franchises check in at the top of the pecking order. Each of the top six teams made at least one trade.

A little further down, the Packers jumped into the top 10 without adding to their roster. A certain superstar edge rusher should return to action by the end of the month, though.

#2505. NFL Week 10 picks, best bets: Steelers cool off Joe Burrow's Bengals, Chiefs roll in Atlanta

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

There's only one way to describe last week in the NFL: Chalk.

Favorites dominated the Week 9 slate as just one upset occurred while every other favorite took care of business. That was music to our ears because we saw the week playing out that exact way, dialing up a perfect 15-0 record on the moneyline. The only underdog we liked last week was Green Bay, and they proved us right as they rolled into Foxborough and steamrolled the Patriots. That not only helped me notch a pristine moneyline record but also cashed one of my five Locks of the Week.

There, I was 3-2 ATS, which jived with my more modest 8-7 ATS record for the week overall. That's not as stellar as the straight-up mark, but we were above .500, so we made money. And that's what we're after at the end of the day.

I'll try to keep the momentum rolling into Week 10 where, unlike last week, I do have a fair share of underdogs pulling off the upsets. That includes the Pittsburgh Steelers, who land inside my five Locks of the Week.

Note: Chicago, Denver, Philadelphia, and Tampa Bay are on the bye in Week 10.

There's arguably no offense hotter right now than the Bengals. Over their four-game winning streak, they've averaged over 35 points per game, and Joe Burrow has been playing at an MVP level. The Cincinnati QB has 18 total touchdowns over this stretch and a 132.0 passer rating. Simply put, they've been a bulldozer. However, I do think it's worth pointing out who they've played over the course of the winning streak: at Dolphins, at Ravens (no Lamar Jackson), vs. Titans and vs. Falcons. Not exactly a murderer's row.

Pittsburgh, who beat these Bengals back in Week 3, should provide much more resistance than what they've faced recently. The Steelers defense is tied for the fifth-lowest yards per play average (5.0), tied for the fourth-lowest points per game allowed (18.0), and tied for the eighth-lowest passer rating allowed (83.3). Meanwhile, Cincinnati's defense is tied for the most yards per rush attempt allowed so far this season (5.0), which sets up Jaylen Warren to continue his ascent as one of the true breakout players of the season.

On top of this being a potential mismatch for the Bengals going up against this stout Steelers team, their scheduling surrounding this game does them no favors either. While they'll be at home in Week 10, Cincinnati is coming off an international game in Madrid last week. As for the Steelers, they're fresh off their bye week, creating a sizable rest discrepancy. All of this is a recipe for an upset.

Projected score: Steelers 27, Bengals 24The pick: Steelers +3.5

While their 3-5 records don't exactly scream playoff contenders, first place in the NFC South is on the line in this game. Bryce Young doesn't have the best history going up against the Saints, as the Panthers quarterback is just 1-5 against his division foe in his career. That said, I think there's a window here for him to get a rare victory against New Orleans on Sunday.

While his numbers have come down since his stellar start to begin the season, Young started to look more like himself in the loss to Denver, completing 71.7% of his passes to go along with three touchdowns. The Saints secondary is allowing 7.3 yards per attempt so far this season, which is tied for the fifth-highest in the league. Their 99.5 passer rating allowed is also the seventh-highest in the NFL. This isn't as daunting a matchup for Young, who had to face Tampa Bay, Green Bay, and Denver over Carolina's recent three-game losing streak. I like him to rebound here.

Meanwhile, New Orleans is 1-4 straight-up and 0-5 ATS at home this season, so the Superdome hasn't been too friendly thus far.

Projected score: Panthers 24, Saints 21The pick: Panthers +1.5

Similar to what we discussed with Cincinnati, the Falcons do have to deal with immediately playing the following week after an international game in Madrid last Sunday. That may only put them further behind the eight ball against a Chiefs team that cruised to a 35-12 win over the Jets last week. Patrick Mahomes did give us all a scare in the midst of that game after injuring his elbow, but it doesn't appear serious enough to keep him out of this matchup.

Mahomes has thrown five touchdowns and no interceptions over his past two games, but his lack of a downfield threat has been noticeable. He's averaging an NFL-low 5.6 air yards per attempt this season as the Chiefs have really looked for pass catches to put up yards after the catch. Well, they just acquired some help in that regard in Josh Downs, whom they brought in before the deadline in a trade with the Colts. The wideout has a knack for creating separation and now has a capable quarterback to deliver the football to him, so Kansas City could see quick dividends from this addition. That's especially true against a Falcons secondary that was just lit up by the Bengals last week and just traded away star safety Jessie Bates III to the Jaguars.

Atlanta is also 0-4 straight-up and ATS in its last four games against the AFC.

Projected score: Chiefs 26, Falcons 20The pick: Chiefs -3.5

Jacksonville went all-in at the deadline, making trades to acquire Jessie Bates III, Jordan Davis and Davon Godchaux to bolster its defense for a potential Super Bowl run. On the flip side, Tennessee traded away pieces, including standout safety Amani Hooker and, going back a couple of weeks, defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons. That's a lot of talent being drained from the defense, which doesn't bode well against Trevor Lawrence, who is making a sneaky MVP push. Entering Week 10, his 111.7 passer rating ranks second among quarterbacks who have started at least eight games, only looking up to Burrow.

As this double-digit spread suggests, this is a David vs. Goliath matchup, and it's hard to imagine the underdog keeping this thing close. Even before making these trades, Jacksonville's defense was allowing 15.1 points per game (second-best in the NFL) and has also allowed 20 or fewer points in six straight road games. Tony Pollard, who remained with the team through the deadline, has been a bright spot in Tennessee's offense in recent weeks, but could be negated here. The Jaguars are allowing 3.7 yards per carry this season, along with an 89.3 rushing yards per game allowed average that ranks fifth-lowest in the NFL.

#2504. Chance Conversion – MH

von Next Generation am 09.09.2025 in den Kategorien Tactical Theory mit 4 Kommentaren

Conversion rate has statistically been proven to be one of the best indicators for predicting a team’s success (Souza et al., 2019). All the more astonishing, then, that the underlying influencing factors are still largely unknown to most, leaving chance conversion for many as something of a black box. This analysis aims to improve the effectiveness and efficiency of goalscoring situations.

Chance conversion is most often associated with mental aspects. Accordingly, after defeats it is sometimes used as an excuse, partly due to a lack of more convincing alternative explanations. After all, the coach is said to have little or no influence on the psychological state of his players. Instead, the players are expected to learn how to better handle the pressure of a goalscoring opportunity, and in doing so become more efficient in front of goal.
